subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BA' GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS

speechtext: Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved the third reading of Bill No. 82, to amend the Bank of Canada Act.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BA' GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is such an important piece of legislation, perhaps one of the most important that has come before any parliament, that on this, the third reading, those of us who did not speak on it previously should I think take advantage of this last opportunity to express our views. I say it is important because, as has already been pointed out, it was an issue in the last election, and the people have looked to this piece of legislation, the new set-up of this bank, the change that was promised with some hope of relief from present economic conditions. During the election Liberal speakers throughout the ridings of this country told the people that if the Liberal party was returned to power the Bank of Canada would be nationalized, taken over by the government and operated in the interests of the people. I think one member, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), went so far as to say in a speech in Vancouver, that, in addition, the Liberal party if returned to power would proceed to issue new money, and he mentioned an amount something like $50,000,000. The provinces, the municipalities and the cities naturally looked upon this proposed change as affording relief from the financial conditions from which they were suffering. They expected that money would circulate more freely. I think that impression was general throughout the country, and that is the reason, Mr. Speaker, I consider this one of the most important pieces of legislation that has come before the house. My reply to these gentlemen who advocated government ownership was this: that to do so was very simple, that the Bank of Canada was set up following the recommendations of a royal commission, and that if any government found that it did not work in the best interests of the people, the set-up of the bank could easily be changed. If that change was to be nationalization of the bank by the government taking it over, that could be accomplished very simply by taking over the stock of the private shareholders.
I think we all agree that what we need is not new money in this country but a greater velocity in the circulation of money. But so far the policy of this government, which has been in office now for six months, has been to adopt measures which tend to block rather than to stimulate the circulation of money. For instance, the Minister of Finance the other day announced that a large loan had been floated, and we all know that a very fine return was offered to investors to come forward and invest in that loan, an interest rate of 3J per cent.

Bank of Canada-Mr. Barber

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: No.

I believe it was close to
that; at all events it was a greater return than could be received from investments in industry to-day. That was one action that was taken by the government that tended to slow up industry. Then we have the eight per cent sales tax, the highest sales tax known in any country, and all you have to do to learn its effects, is to inquire in business circles, where you will find that it has tended to slow up the circulation of the dollar.
I wish to refer now to one particular section of the bill, section 15. I approach this with a full knowledge that it is a subject upon which harsh words have been spoken and one which has caused bitter feeling in different parts of this country, but I believe this is the place to discuss it, not in the little red sehoolhouse or on the back lines. I shall say what I have to say with the greatest moderation because I do not think anyone can accuse me of being intolerant in such matters.
I have the greatest respect and the greatest regard for our friends the French speaking Canadians of this country. I do not think anyone has a greater respect for them. I have made many friends amongst them since being here, and I hope they will take the remarks I make to-day in the spirit in which they are made, with the greatest of moderation. I was pleased to hear an hon. member from a town in the province of Quebec tell us the other evening how splendidly the French
speaking and English speaking people of his town get along together; how for a long time they elected alternately a French speaking and then an English speaking mayor. That is a wonderful spirit; it is the spirit we must have between the two great races in Canada if we are to make this country what it should be. But I could not figure out just what that had to do with the question of bilingual currency in the year 1936. I say to the members of this house, and I say it in all earnestness, knowing this country pretty well, that I see great danger in this particular section at this time, a time when our people are suffering perhaps as they have never suffered before from economic conditions. I believe that this section is the sowing of seed that is bound to grow into an issue in this country which will be perhaps more serious than anything that has happened since confederation, something that will not be in the interests of harmony between the two great races and that will not be in the best interests of the minority in this country.
Just look at the picture, for instance, of western Canada. In the province from which I come, British Columbia, the French speaking population is less than three per cent; in Alberta the French speaking population is less than six per cent; in Saskatchewan it is less than six per cent, and in Manitoba it is less than seven per cent. I think I will put this table of figures on Hansard. It is based on the 1931 census and comes from the bureau of statistics:

That shows quite a different picture from the one given the other evening by an hon. member from one of the ridings in the province of Quebec, and I think it is something that should be taken into consideration very seriously by this house.
I want to make this one statement. I do not believe that in this whole world there is a more tolerant people than the English speaking people of Canada. They have tolerated, in the past-I am going to put it that way- bilingual postage stamps, issued without any authority of parliament. They have tolerated the forms that were referred to by the Minister of Finance the other night, issued with-
[Mr. Barber.l
out the authority of parliament. As some hon. gentlemen know, they have in many sections protested strenuously against French announcements over the radio, with the result that they have been moderated. No English speaking member has stood on his feet in this house and said that as this is not according to the constitution, it should be removed. No; it was tolerated. Now with the authority of parliament we are going to provide that this is a bilingual country, that we are to have bilingual currency in circulation throughout the country. I warn the government and hon. members of this house that that will not create the harmony and cooperation that we

Bank of Canada-Mr. Barber
want to see between the two great races in Canada. I hope and trust it will never be- ' come a political issue, although it may be forced as an issue by the people.
I should like to quote from Hansard of 1905 in order to give a clear picture of how the Liberal party stood on this question. I refer to page 6026 of Hansard of May 21, 1905. The following questions were asked of Mr. Fielding, then Minister of Finance
1.	Do any grave reasons of state exist that might prevent the Minister of Finance from having the dominion one dollar and two dollar notes or all other bank notes printed simultaneously in English and French?
2.	Are they unaware in the finance department that the two languages are official in Canada?
3.	Is it the intention of the Minister of Finance to rectify in the future this state of things by ordering that those bank notes be printed in both languages, English and French?
Mr. Fielding answered as follows:
There is nothing in the British North America Act or in any act of the parliament of Canada, which requires or contemplates the printing of dominion notes in two languages.
The finance department has not contemplated the advisability of any departure from the practice which has existed under all governments from the beginning of confederation down to the present time.
That was the official statement of the Liberal party in 1905. When the present act was framed consideration was given by parliament to our French speaking Canadians for the first time in the history of this country. This act provides that notes of the Bank of Canada be printed in the French language as well as English. A large number of French speaking people live in the constituency which I have had the honour to represent for a number of years and I have never heard any objection on their part to receiving money printed in their own language. I do not think there has been any protest from the great masses of French speaking Canadians against money being printed in the French language. The provision in the present act has been working only about a year and it has not -been given a chance.
The main argument of the minister is that it cost about $29,000 to print these bills in the French language. I have not heard any protest from any English speaking member of this house against the cost. Further, there has never been a protest from any English speaking member or from anyone else in Canada that I have heard of against the expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars spent in printing the proceedings of this house and the publications of the different departments in the French language. That was provided for and there has been no complaint. There has been no objection to that from the English speaking people. Is this action going to return to us the $29,000? No, it means that we are going to spend at least another $29,000 to print the new money. I think even some hon. members to my left will agree that that money could be spent to greater advantage these days.
The people of the two great races are not demanding a new dollar; they are demanding that they be given the opportunity to earn a dollar. They are not particular whether that dollar is new; they are prepared to accept the dollars that have been provided. What they want is an opportunity to earn a dollar. The great army of the unemployed want work in order that they may earn a dollar. Merchants, business men, farmers and citizens generally throughout this country are in dire need of purchasing power through the circulation of more dollars. I say to hon. members of this house: Instead of bringing up an issue like this at the present time, the spending of money which the Minister of Finance has complained about, let us, as the representatives of the people of Canada unite in an effort to try to improve conditions by assisting Canadians from one end of this great country to the other. I say to the house that the bringing up of an issue of this kind and the forcing of bilingual currency upon the great majority of English speaking people is not in the best interests of Canada as a whole.
I want to make one last appeal to the individual members of the house because it is the individual members who should decide these matters. I hope it will never -become a party question, but this is a question that is put up to every individual member. It is not a question of the rights of the minority or the rights of the majority; it is a matter which should be considered in the light of present day conditions. It has been stated that the printing of the French bills cost $29,000. therefore it stands to reason that we shall have to spend at least $29,000 more. Is that wise? That money might better be spent in some other way. There has been no protest from the great masses of French speaking Canadians against the issue of bills printed in French. This has come from a group or organization of which we have heard during the last five years. A determined effort has been made, irrespective of the wishes of Canadians as a whole, to force bilingualism on this country. The thin end of the wedge has been driven in. As I have stated already, we have the bilingual postage stamp, which has been tolerated, but I fear the great masses of English speaking people will not

I think the leader of the opposition, in speaking the other
day, was right in laying a certain stress on freedom of choice. He mentioned two circumstances which should govern in the matter of a decision. One was that there should be freedom of choice with respect to the question whether a citizen wished to accept a document or bill in English or in French, and he said that the course which should be adopted was the one which would further, to the greatest extent, harmony and good will among the different elements in the country. He referred to the documents on the table of the House of Commons and said, "They are here, some in French and some in English. Hon. members may come and take whichever they please." Certainly they have real freedom of choice in that regard and can take which they please. But what freedom of choice has a citizen who is being paid a debt or wishes to settle an account or is receiving payment of an account-what freedom of choice has he as regards the acceptance of money that may be offered him if it happens to be in French or English as the case may be and he prefers the other denomination? The only freedom of choice is to see, whether he be English speaking or French speaking, that he be given a bill which is acceptable to him because of its clearness in reference to the denomination and other essential details. If the intention were to obliterate from the face of a bill the descriptive wording where in English or, on the other hand, to obliterate the descriptive wording where in French, there might be objection to a course of that kind. But where those of the English speaking part of the population are given the opportunity to obtain a bill with all essential details printed entirely in English, I cannot see what possible objection there can be to permitting on that same bill similar information in French for those who happen to be of French origin.
As to harmony and good will, surely an attitude of the kind which recognizes natural desires and needs is likely to promote a better feeling than an attitude of intolerance which will not permit anything of the sort. I point out, however, to my fellow countrymen who are of French origin and speak the French language that those who will take the evidence of history for what it may be worth -and it is fairly important-will find that wherever the granting of a privilege or a concession by a majority has by the minority been crystallized into a right, resulting in a pushing of the demand beyond those moderate and reasonable boundaries that have marked the maintenance of harmonious relations between majorities and minorities, the consequence has been harmful to the minority.
That is the first paragraph I desire to quote. I do so for the reason that it speaks about the granting of a privilege or a concession by a majority to a minority. I wish to

say that any right which the French speaking portion of our country enjoy with respect to bilingual postal notes or to bilingual postage or anything else of the kind has not been in the nature of a concession or of a privilege conferred by parliament. It has been in the nature of a recognition of the full rights of Canadian citizenship.
My right hon. friend goes on to say:
Why not let the demand for a change come about by that gradual process which would ensure that those who are most affected, namely, the majority, who are of British descent and speak the English language, will feel, as they do not now feel, the desire to do something further in a spirit of amity and good will ?	.

In speaking to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber), which I second, I trust that I shall be considered moderate in my arguments; and I shall appeal to the house, not from the standpoint of partyism or of race or creed, but in a broadminded way, as any true Canadian citizen should.
When in 1935 the Bank of Canada came into being, certain definite functions were assigned to it. It is not necessary for me to review these at the present time; the matter was well debated on the resolution and when the bill was in committee. Suffice it to say that I think the act as constituted should have had a fair and reasonable trial, to ascertain whether the bank could perform the functions that were delegated to it. One of its powers was that of issuing separate notes, that is, notes in English and notes in French. I believe that last Friday the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and to-day the hon. member for Fraser Valley, have made appeals for this system of issuing the currency as constituted under the act, and that it should have a fair chance to be tried out, to see what value it has, as it was no doubt a gesture of good will to the French speaking people. I think that suggestion was worthy of consideration. All hon. members who sat in the last parliament well remember the debate that took place when the bill was introduced last session. We recall the definite statement that was made by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), then the leader of the opposition. We also all remember the discussions that took place during the campaign in September and October last, when the Liberal party, and in particular its leader, made definite promises to the people of Canada that if they were returned to power they would make certain changes in the act. These are the amendments that they now propose. Hon. members on the government side must surely have expected criticism of those amendments from this side, and especially from the extreme left hand corner. Some of them also may well have expected criticism from among their own members;
and recently they have listened to very stinging criticism and condemnation from one of their own supporters, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). I do not think any better language could have been used than was employed by him to describe the betrayal by the government of the people of Canada. I state what is known to all members of this house, that during the last campaign bilingual notes was not an issue; the matter was never discussed, even last session when the bill was before the house. In my opinion the government, by this amendment, is betraying the people of Canada just as much as it did by not going the full limit in some other respects as stated by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.
It was stated when the bill was in committee that nothing should be done to raise the racial question, and that statement has been made to-day also. I do not believe any member of this house really wants to say anything that will raise any racial question at this time; far from it, but I think the interpretation the people of Canada will place on the speech delivered by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) last week and the speech delivered to-day by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will be that those two addresses will go a long way towards raising that racial question. We are all proud of this great confederation. Each province has made its contribution; both the English speaking and the French speaking Canadians have done their share, and the special consideration that was shown the French speaking people in having bills printed in English and French certainly was a gesture of good will designed to further consolidate our confederation. In his speech the Minister of Justice quoted from an address delivered by the great Conservative Prime Minister, the late Sir John A. Macdonald, in 1890 with regard to the use of the two languages. If I cared to take time to read that quotation I think hon. members would see that it had no reference at all to bilingual currency or for that matter currency of any kind. My reply to the Minister of Justice would be to quote from a speech delivered by one who, I think the Liberals will agree, was the greatest Liberal prime minister Canada has- ever had, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I refer to a speech made seventeen years after the addTess by Sir John A. Macdonald to which reference has been made. In replying to an appeal made by Mr. Lavergne, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, according to Hansard for February 25, 1907, at page 3655:
But to affirm, as he does-
That is, Mr. Lavergne.



Bank oj Canada-Mr. Parley
-that the French language should be used upon every occasion, and that every public document should be printed on one side in French and the other side in English, is, I think, going a little too far. For instance, I understand that my hon. friend wants bank notes to be printed either in French or in English. For my part I never yet saw an occasion when a bank note printed in English was not properly understood by the French people; and I am quite sure that a bank note printed in French would be understood by the English people to be exactly what it means.
That is exactly the condition we have at present under this act.

These people naturally cannot understand the special considerations or gestures, call them what you will, that we are extending to the French speaking people from time to time, when our

Bank of Canada-Mr. Church
constitution does not provide for Canada to be a bilingual country. It was with difficulty last year that we explained the special privilege or gesture of good will that we extended by having the notes printed in English and French. There is no doubt that if this amendment passes we may before many years have a protest from this class of people, and a demand that they have some consideration for their native tongue. The debate that took place in the last parliament on the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) will be within the memory of many hon. members. Also we can well remember the debates that took place in 1935. Hon. members who were members of the banking and commerce committee that considered the bill in 1935 will remember the discussion that took place in that committee. It was purely as a gesture of good will that it was provided that the bank notes should be available in one or other of the two languages where required. This surely places French and English on an equality, as the Minister of Justice appealed for. There never has been a question in respect to equality. I am sure no hon. member can point to any debate that ever took place in this house and I cannot think of any since I have been in it that raised the question of equality. We have always been proud of the contribution made by the French speaking people to confederation. The wording of this bill however will do much to raise the racial question, of which we are all fearful. It presents more evidence of the possibility of raising the racial question than any other measure that has ever passed in this house.
In conclusion I plead with the Minister of Finance to endeavour to persuade the government not to press this amendment providing for bilingual notes. I hope I have dealt with the question in a spirit of fair play and in the manner of a true Canadian citizen. Certainly I am not one who wants to raise any racial question in Canada at the present time. I therefore second the amendment moved by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, that the bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of striking out section 15.

speechtext:
I do not intend to give a silent vote on the third reading of this bill. When the order was called I had intended to oppose the Bank of Canada bill on general grounds, and if after this amendment is voted down anyone moves a six months' hoist of the whole bill I shall vote for that.
12739-239J
I was very much surprised to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the name of the Liberal party make the speech he did after the address he made in this house on the same legislation on June 22, 1934. In connection with the rights of minorities and majorities in this country we have reached this state of affairs, that a militant minority can coerce the majority. That is what we have come to under confederation to-day. The Prime Minister said in the House Commons a week ago last Thursday in connection with another bill:
The principle I am laying down is that there is no minority which is superior to the majority, and that majority is the people of the country as a whole; and the people of the country as a whole have sent this present House of Commons to legislate.
Well, may I say in answer to the right hon. gentleman that this House of Commons was not sent by the people of this country to vote for this Bank of Canada bill, or for section 15 of it. The government had no mandate from Ontario for this bill. We are now in the sixty-ninth year of confederation. During that time successive governments, Liberal and Conservative, have presided over the affairs of Canada; various parliaments have been elected; there have been various prime ministers and ministers of finance, yet we in all that long time had to wait until 1936 for the first minister of finance to rise in this house and say that the bank bills of the dominion, namely dominion notes of one and two dollar's, are to be printed in English and French and that French is to be placed on an equality with English throughout the dominion-something that the fathers of confederation never intended; a thing against the spirit and letter of confederation; something on which the people of this country have never had a chance to express an opinion.
As I have said, the history of the world is the history of minorities. The history of this country is the history of compromises. Confederation was a compromise. One compromise was regarding bilingualism, the use of French and English. These rights are set out in section 133 of the British North America Act, as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act. and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
3756	COMMONS
Bank of Canada-Mr. Church
That was a compromise and was to be a finality without any extensions. It was intended at that time that there should be no extension of the rights and privileges granted under section 133. Whether or not the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) or the Prime Minister thinks this is a political question, there is no doubt it is a political question, and whether they like it or not it is going to be a political question until it is settled right. No question is settled in this country until it is settled according to justice and according to the terms of confederation, and this thing is going to be open until it is settled, and the door is not closed yet by any means.
It is no-t my purpose to speak at length at this time, but I wish to register my protest. I do not speak for the Conservative party; I speak as a private member of parliament sent here to do his duty. Representing the constituency I do, I deem it my duty to oppose the third reading of this bill. I should not be doing my duty if I failed to oppose this two-faced Doctor Jekyll and Mr. Hyde bill. This bill is not public ownership at all, it is something in the election which the Prime Minister and other members of the Liberal party promised the country if elected. There can be no control without ownership. The pledge given by the government for a publicly owned bank has not been fulfilled. It is a political bill much more than a banking or economic bill. It is called a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act, but it might better be called a Barnurn and Bailey bill; it is neither public ownership nor public control, for there is no control without total ownership. It does not amend the Bank of Canada act, but it makes a scrap of paper out of the Bank of Canada Act of 1934, and violates the principle of section 133 of the British North America Act, which I quoted.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier never wrould have sanctioned this bill. He always acted on this question with great prudence and diplomacy, but where is there evidence of prudence or diplomacy here? Was it ever discussed in the election campaign? No, not one word. My friends cannot show any such discussion from February 25, 1907, when the former member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) proposed a motion in this house for equality of treatment of the two Languages, on which occasion Sir Wilfrid Laurier did express certain opinions. Sir Wilfrid Laurier stood here as Prime Minister. Mr. Fielding took the same stand for many years. Neither would ever propose such a bill as this or support it, or ever bring it up on the decennial revision of the Bank Act.
This bill offers no help in solving the social and economic problems of this country. There is no proposal in it to have a limited amount

of controlled inflation up to fifty or a hundred million dollars to take care of the unemployed, to take care of a reconstruction, housing and slum clearance program, and dear knows it was badly needed this spring in the large cities so as to get people off the dole and back to work. There is nothing in this bill about that. It will make no improvement over the past in our economic conditions. A partly privately owned and partly publicly owned institution will get Canada nowhere if there is no control.
Regarding the inspection clause, we had a case the other day of a government official taking the interest on deposits and putting it in his pockets in spite of all the inspection.
This bank is a political bank; that is all it is and all it will become in time; nothing but a glorified Home bank. Wait till you see what happens. Wait till you see it next year. If it does not end up by being that, it will be no fault of the framers of the bill. The bill is a victory, no doubt, for the bankers' association and for St. James street and for the chartered banks. I can see the fine hand of these great interests in this bill, whether others can see it or not. I have studied this question and I can see it. These people have at last been successful in their efforts to cripple any effective central bank and to undo the good work already done.
Section 15 enables the letter and spirit of confederation to be made a scrap of paper; that is all it is. If the government want to give the minority these rights under confederation, let them do it in the proper legal way. Let them come in at the front door, not at the side door. Let them open and amend section 133 of the' British North America Act, regarding the use of the French language instead of sliding this thing through in a minor bank act. Let them come in by the front door of the House of Commons and bring in a bill to amend the British North America Act, section 133, to extend the rights and privileges and prerogatives of the French language in this country.
The Minister of Justice says that the bilingual notes are necessary because they will be deposited in the courts of Quebec, and that these bank notes are legal tender. But, Mr. Speaker, the practice of the courts with reference to deposits is changing to marked cheques and certificates from trust companies; certified cheques are being used, and there are many other ways of depositing legal tender in the various official judicial offices of this country. For the Minister of Justice to use that as a leading argument, therefore, is only begging the question.

Bank of Canada-Mr. Church
Section 15 is a victory for a militant minority, coercing a passive majority that is too proud to fight, too proud to stand up for its rights either in this house or out of it. We have a press, pulpit and legislature that is too proud to fight along the line of defending the rights and prerogatives of majorities. The recent investigation at Washington showed how the banks and big interests have been coercing the press of that country. Why do you see so little in the press, in the English speaking papers of this country, about section 15? Twenty-five years ago what a rebellion *there would have been if a minority was going to saddle a majority along the lines that this bill does? The evidence at Washington that was given in the press showed how the banks and big interests and departmental stores in the United States had trammelled a free press, and had warned them that they would cut out their advertisements. We heard something about that even in Canada happening in the first days of this parliament. But for an able press, things would have been ten times worse than they are in this country, and I am here to endeavour to support and protect a free press from such attacks. It is all right to drive a coach and four through the British North America Act, as section 15 of this bill does, to please some people, but we cannot get a section of the British North America Act amended for the purpose of getting progress in this country, and getting the working _ class out of the strait-jacket which the British North America Act has put around them, and which the courts help to keep them in at times.
It is said that those who oppose section 15 are bringing this thing into politics. Did you ever hear anything like that in your life? Of course it is bound to be in politics and to stay in politics until it is repealed, and those who brought it into polities are hon. gentlemen opposite. They are the first ones in sixty-nine years who have proposed that these dominion notes-for that is all they are, these ones and twos and so forth under the old legislation-shall be printed in the two languages.
There was a provision made by section 24, subsection 4, of chapter 43 of the statutes of 1934, the Bank of Canada Act:
The form and material of the notes shall be subject to approval by the minister: Provided that notes in either the English or the French language shall be available as required.
That worked out all right in practice. I was not a member of the house in 1934 when the Bank of Canada Act was passed, but at the same time it worked out all right in practice, and those who wanted notes in
English or in French could get them at the different branches, but if I had been in the house at the time as a member I would have opposed even this concession.
As to what the Minister of Justice says about the notes being legal tender in the law courts, I was making inquiries of a number of people connected with the law courts and I find that there are many other ways of making deposits than by depositing actual five-dollar bills in the courts. The trust companies and banks and law societies have made a change.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, is unworthy of Liberalism. This is not a bilingual country. Sir Wilfrid Laurier admitted it was not, and there have been decisions of the courts to the same effect. It is a country in which by section 133 of the British North America Act two languages are official. I want to congratulate the right hon. leader of the opposition upon rising in his place and speaking in the face of great opposition as he did the other day, as a statesman. I believe the words he spoke will prove in the years to come to have been proven prophecy. What he said will come true, and application made will be, session after session, to repeal section 15.
In my opinion we should never have had any provincial legislatures at all. They were the creation of the fathers of confederation for political and not economic purposes, and have been at the root of all the race and religious jealousies in Canada. They do not have them in Great Britain; their powers are limited in the United States, and the result is that in these countries they are one people without the racial and religious jealousies which this country has had. The leader of the opposition has been consistent. I have read his speech of June 22, 1934. The leader of this government sat in parliament as Prime Minister for nine years, from 1921 to 1930, and did he ever propose a section like this? No. It is only when he has a majority behind him of about 170 that he is ready to go over the heads of the electors. Did he tell them anything about this in the election? If he had said it in the election he would not have had five seats in the province of Ontario, because majorities, while they are sleepy and slow to assert their rights and privileges, once they are aroused are going to have something to say. Canada is not and never was a bilingual country. It is a country where the two languages are official languages, but the law courts have set out the length and depth and breadth of the two languages as defined in section 133 of the British North America Act. It is all very well to say that those
3758	COMMONS
Bank of Canada-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
who oppose this bill are doing so for political purposes. I say it is no use for the representatives of the majority to sit here and enact the part of a scarecrow, and allow a false face to be put on them by this bill. A false face is being put upon the majority of the people of this country with an inscription in one language on one side of our bills and an inscription in another language on the other side. It will be just like a patent medicine advertisement which is printed in both languages, or a racing tip or other things of this sort. Those who vote for this bill vote for bilingualism for posterity, to-day and forever.
This particular legislation will be here forever. Those who vote for this bill are voting that this country is to be a bilingual country by order of a militant minority. The people of Ontario are opposed to this, and I am opposed to it. Hon. members should act like men. They should stand by their principles and acquit themselves like men and be strong, say to certain of those hon. members who come from Ontario that they would not be here to-day if in the last election they had proposed a bill like this. Some hon. gentlemen come from western Ontario, some from northern Ontario and others from central Ontario, and I ask them to acquit themselves like men, to be free citizens and free members of parliament, to assert their rights and privileges as private members instead of sitting in their seats and allowing a coach and four to be driven through the principles of confederation by a militant minority for the first time in sixty-nine years.
May I say to hon. gentlemen that I would rather be defeated because of my principles, as I was in 1930 than to sit in this house and force bilingualism on the people of the province of Ontario over their heads and without their knowledge or consent. That is my answer to hon. gentlemen who are opposing what I have to say. There is no such thing as compromise in connection with a great principle; this thing permits of no compromise. The question cannot be settled until it is settled in the right way.
I see the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) in his seat. On many occasions his utterances are filled with common sense, and I refer hon. members to his remarks about the British North America Act, made the other night in connection with another bill. At that time he said he would go to another place and use his influence, and I hope he will go to another place immediately and use a little extra influence in connection with this matter. This bill is a credit to Ottawa, the headquarters of pacifism and pussyfooting.

Ottawa never knows what the rest of the country is thinking. The only things militant I can see about Ottawa are the mosquitoes which infest this building.
I do not care whether I am here for a long time or a short time; I am ready always to stand by my principles. As long as I am here I intend to speak what I believe to be the truth, honestly, fairly and moderately. I am opposed to this legislation. I have always been opposed to the extension of this principle in this country. While I wear the party uniform-I will never be able to wear its plush-I will do my duty in the ranks, but it will be as a volunteer and not as a conscript. In conclusion, I want to congratulate that very able statesman, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) for the manner in which he opposed this bill the other night and for the words of wisdom which he uttered on that occasion. I believe that in the future those words will prove to be a force in this country and become proven prophecy.

The bank notes of Canada go to other countries-to the United States, to France and to continental countries. Do you think that a bank note all in French, as it is at the present time, circulated in France or Belgium or elsewhere, gives to the people of those countries a true picture of Canada? I have only this to say in conclusion. We have the privilege of speaking the two greatest languages in the world. When you go to Geneva you find in the League of Nations these two official languages spoken, and the Canadian delegates are proud to be there representing the only country in the world where the two official languages of that body, representing all the nations on the globe, are spoken. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, when these bank notes circulate throughout the world they will represent what Canada is, a country that was founded by French pioneers and later ceded to the British, a country where the descendants of these two great races succeeded1 in burying their differences and their difficulties and in uniting for the purpose of building a truly great nation. The people of this country are not afraid to let the world know that these two languages are spoken in Canada, languages of which anyone might well be proud; they are not afraid to let it be known that this condition exists in this dominion. I do believe, however, that on this occasion the issues have been exaggerated beyond their true proportions. As a Canadian I should like to see every citizen able to speak both official languages. It is one of my own regrets that I am not able to speak French, but I trust that the generation that will follow me will not suffer from that deficiency. Anyone who listened to the speech delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon and listened particularly to the eloquent address of the Minister of Justice the other evening must have been moved by the fervent plea made for racial unity in Canada. With that sentiment of the Minister of Justice and those associated with him, I wish to join one hundred1 per cent. This country is made up of a great many racial minorities, and in my opinion if we treat those minorities even in a generous spirit, Canada as a whole will be more than amply repaid for making that gesture towards those who may be of foreign origin in the dominion. I think it would be a gross mistake if the house were to accept the suggestion which the amendment puts forward and delete from-the bill the clause it now contains. For my part I intend to vote against the amendment.
May I say a word in another direction. Perhaps it is not necessary for me to remind the house that I belong to a very ancient race, a race whose history has been through the centuries a most painful one and who even at the present time are suffering intense persecution in different parts of the world. Those who belong to the same race as myself appreciate more than they can express in words the measure of justice and tolerance they have received under British rule. In regard to the matter now before us I do wish to express a sentiment that is rather different. There is at this time, unfortunately, particularly in the province of Quebec, a sentiment that is being expressed openly, both by word and in the newspapers, that has not merely the semblance of intolerance but also the idea of inflaming one race against the other, and I do feel, in view of the discussion that has taken place on the floor of the house this afternoon, and the eloquent plea made by the Minister of Justice the other evening on behalf of -his French speaking compatriots, that perhaps that wave of anti-Semitism which to-day seems to be showing itself in certain quarters of Quebec will diminish if not entirely

These are about the only remarks I wish to make at the present time. I simply wish to make a plea for racial unity in Canada, so that all sections of the population may go forward and try to make Canada a country worthy not only of the present but also of future generations.

In advancing his argument the Minister of Justice referred to three other countries in which there is bilingual money. Of course I always feel that other countries can do as they please. In developing his argument the minister said, as I understood him, that the conditions in those countries were approximately or largely the same as they are in Canada. I propose to
give some particulars about each one of those countries, namely, Belgium, Switzerland, and South Africa. There are something over eight million people in Belgium, and they are all packed into a little over eleven thousand square miles. Rather more than three million speak German and somewhat less than three million speak French. A million speak both languages. Belgium could be packed into the small portion of Ontario extending from Toronto to Brockville, east and west, and from Toronto to the Severn river, north and south. The area is small, and the conditions in Belgium are not really comparable, as I shall endeavour to show a little later, with those of Canada.
Switzerland has an area of less than sixteen thousand square miles. Twenty-one per cent of its population is French, seventy-one per cent German, and seven per cent Italian. The government of their cantons is entirely different from our conditions in Canada; they are loosely held together, although they have been confederated a long time, and, as the minister said, they do print their bills in three languages. But the country is less than two hundred and fifty miles long and less than one hundred and thirty-five miles wide. In South Africa there are seven million coloured people, natives of Africa, and 1,400,000 whites, of whom, that is the whites, fifty-one per cent speak both languages-that is the Afrikander and the English. Twenty-five per cent are British who speak English only, and twenty-four per cent

plus the fraction in each case-speak only the Afrikander language. Conditions in these countries do not at all compare, along the lines to which I have alluded, with those that obtain in Canada, where we have a country 3,500 miles from east to west and 1,500 miles from north to south, part of it, of course, very sparsely settled; where people who speak English almost exclusively, reside in the main in eight of the provinces, and those who speak the French language are very largely in one province. Therefore conditions here are not the same as in the countries to which the minister has referred. For my part, I can read the bills whether they are printed in French or in both languages. I appreciate, too, some of the arguments that have been advanced by the Minister of Justice in this regard, but on the other hand I believe it would have been better to leave this matter where it was until it had received a fair trial.

If I were to recommend a change in that system I might go back to the method recommended by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but always having been actuated by the spirit of fair play I cannot answer that question in any other way. I repeat, however, that it would have been much better to leave the matter where it was. The previous government had to face this issue just as the present government are attempting to face it, and that issue having been settled it should not have been brought up again, at least not so soon. I doubt very much whether the government have had resolutions asking a change from the chambers of commerce or boards of trade of Vancouver, Halifax, Edmonton, Regina, Winnipeg, Fort William, Windsor, London, Sarnia-where the distinguished whip comes from-Hamilton, Toronto, Belleville, Brockville, Kingston, Saint John, Charlottetown and such cities. If the government have had resolutions from these chambers of commerce or boards of trade asking that the act be amended, that might account for this action having been taken, but I do not believe that is the reason for it. I am convinced that the Minister of Justice is very largely, if not altogether, responsible for persuading, in his pleasant way, the other members of the cabinet to agree to this amendment, because it was the Minister of Justice who in 1934 moved an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act in terms similar to those now contained in this amending bill. So I believe the minister must take all the credit, or whatever else may be due, for any heat that may develop as a result of this amendment.
The other evening the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) said something about Japan and China having bilingual bills. The hon. member knows full well that the bills printed in two languages in China apply to Shanghai and Hongkong, that the bill circulated in the provinces of China, away from the coast, are printed entirely in Chinese. I cannot picture bills circulating in the city of Chengtu in the province of Szechwan, 2,800 miles up the Yangtze-Kiang river being in two languages, when there is only one race of people. Furthermore, according to my understanding on the Japanese bill there is just the word "yen." That is not an English word; it is an international word, and it appears on Japanese bills for the convenience of people of all nations. The word could be claimed as French, German or Czechoslovakian as easily as it could be claimed to be English. 
They do not have bilingual bills in the United States, where they have more Germans than anywhere else in the world outside of Germany. They do not have bilingual bills in France, where there are more Italians than anywhere else in the world except the United States and Italy. There are no bilingual bills in Great Britain, where there are many hundreds of thousands of people of many races. So I do not see just how that can be used as an argument.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I come back to where I began: In my opinion it would have been much better if the government had let this matter rest for a while and left the act as it was passed by the late government. In my humble opinion the previous government met the problem in a satisfactory way. Certainly if bills are to be printed in both languages for circulation in the other eight provinces the government will have to take the responsibility. I cannot say what will be the result, or whether there will be any result, but with others who have spoken I feel that, with the distress which prevails in the country and the difficulties that all of us are up against, as Canadians, it would have been much better to leave the provision as it was, and for that reason I shall vote against section 15 of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, it is with some trepidation that I rise this afternoon to speak on this question. We have been sitting here for some five months, and during that period we have debated a number of very important issues. With the exception of one or two other occasions, however, not until to-day have I felt such a tense atmosphere as exists in the house this afternoon, and in my opinion that is a reflection upon the parliament of Canada.
I come from the province of Saskatchewan. My mind goes back to 1930 and a few years prior to that. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), when he introduced' this measure into the house, referred feelingly to the campaign of 1930. I have every sympathy with him in such feelings. I took no part in the particular controversy at that time. But I want to point out that we in western Canada, fortunately, have emerged from the division upon racial and religious lines which existed then, a division fostered and kept alive, I believe, for political purposes. I regret exceedingly that this matter should have been injected into this new parliament at a time when what we need in Canada is unity of all our people, regardless of race or religion. Today once again we are in danger of having the same kind of thing said and done throughout Canada as was said and done in the years to which I have referred. It is so easy to divert public attention from issues that are real and fundamental by dividing it upon lines that are unreal and not fundamental. The people of Canada are now facing tremendous problems. In this bill we have discussed only one phase of one important problem, namely the national ownership of the Bank of Canada. This house does not yet know, nor has it decided upon the policy to be followed by that bank in relation to currency and credit; but this afternoon, on the motion for third reading of this bill, instead of discussing that important matter we are spending our time in dividing the people on an issue which in my opinion is unreal. I would suggest this, that people in Canada who speak French are entitled1 to have a bank note which they understand, printed in their own language, and the people of the rest of Canada are entitled to demand a bill printed in their common tongue, the English language. If we are going to extend this
principle indefinitely then I point out that in the province from which I come, as was stated by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), we have many nationalities. We have a very large percentage of Germans, some Poles, many Ukrainians, and in that province those people may possibly ask for the same privilege that is now being proposed in relation to another language. I know, of course, there is a difference.

The difference is that, written into our constitution, and quite properly so, there is a provision that the use of the two languages in certain documents and in certain matters and places is established in this country. But I point out that in this present matter we are simply placing in the hands of people who will not scruple to use it, a document that will be shown on many ai public platform in Saskatchewan, and possibly in Manitoba and Alberta, with the probable result of very much the same sort of campaign as was conducted in western Canada in 1930. From my place in this house I say to the government and to the opposition that divisions along these lines are not only regrettable but reprehensible. I make this suggestion to the government; if we cannot agree, why not drop the language from the bill altogether? Why not print on the face of these bills the word "Canada" which is the name of our country in both languages, and with that word simply the numerals 1, 2, 5, or 10 and so on, and distinguish the bills by variation in colour and design? Then we end this controversy, a controversy which in my opinion is kept alive purely for political purposes. I am not accusing any member of the government or of the opposition of doing that at this time, but at least there is a strong suspicion among some hon. members in this comer of the house that there may be motives of that sort. Whether there be such motives or not, this division will be carried throughout the length and breadth of Canada. I am urging the house to face the real problems of the country, problems that are stupendous, problems of youth, problems of the aged, problems of western agriculture. Instead of spending our time in permitting the stirring up of race prejudice we should get down to a thorough consideration of the real problems that confront us.

I may say to my hon.
friend that I could answer him if I so desired, but I am going to ignore such interruptions because I am very anxious to express my thoughts on this matter without heat and without emotion. I think when the Prime Minister suggested that because some one used the word "toleration" or the expression "tolerating certain things which existed," that one might as well make it applicable to the French speaking members of the House of Commons, he indulged in the most specious sophistry. Any man in this country, no matter what his language or his native tongue may be, has a right, a constitutional right by law, to be a member of this House of Commons provided !he is a British subject and complies with the other requirements of the law, and on that basis we all here accept all our fellow-members, not in toleration, but in welcome, even when they may disagree with us in our opinions.
I am anxious to place on record my thoughts on this subject, and I shall be sorry if, having done so, I should find myself classified in that category which the right hon. the Prime Minister described as

those having an attitude of intolerance and bigotry. With much of what the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) said to-day I agree. I am one of those who, coming from a part of Ontario in which we rarely if ever hear the French language spoken, have gone to considerable trouble and effort to acquire some knowledge of that language. I, too, like the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) could write out and read in this chamber a speech in French, but by doing so, Mr. Speaker, I should lend neither wisdom to my thoughts nor eloquence to my tongue. Therefore I am going to endeavour to express my thoughts in my native tongue as dispassionately as I may.
The Minister of Justice took occasion to extend the quotation from Sir Wilfrid Laurier which had been quoted by some other member of the house. I possibly could also extend both by prefix and affix a quotation which was given by the Minister of Justice of the words of the great, revered leader of the Conservative party. The subject matter under discussion in 1890 was the question whether or not a provision which had been made allowing the use of the French language in the Northwest Territories should be repealed, and Mr. McCarthy of that day had moved for its repeal. Then Mr. Laurier made a strong political attack upon the government of the day, alleging in effect -I am not quoting him but I am giving the substance-that the Tories had always been opposed to the French people and the interests of the French people in this country, and it was on that occasion and replying to that speech that Sir John A. Macdonald said:
I go a great way with my hon. friend in his remarks concerning the principle of this bill.
That is the bill which was before the house.
I sympathize with his very natural feelings of indignation at much of the language that has been used in support of this measure now before the house.
Then he used the words quoted by my hon. friend1 the Minister of Justice, and after using them said:
But while I say so much, Mr. Speaker, I must regret that my hon. friend, perhaps yielding to the necessity of his position as a party leader, should have commenced his speech with some party attacks against the Tories.
Sir John A. Macdonald then went on to outline that there should be given to the people of the Northwest Territories the right of free choice, and ultimately there was proposed by Sir John Thompson, and voted on and supported and carried by the government of that day the following resolution in amendment of

Bank oj Canada-Mr. Lawson
the proposal of Mr. McCarthy which I previously outlined:
That, on the contrary, this house declares its adherence to the said covenants, and its determination to resist any attempt to impair the same. That, at the same time, this house deems it expedient and proper, and not inconsistent with those covenants, that the legislative assembly of the Northwest Territories should receive from the parliament of Canada power to regulate-
Note this, Mr. Speaker:
-after the next general elections of the assembly the proceedings of the assembly and the manner of recording and publishing such proceedings.
To that principle of free choice if that is inherently a principle of the Conservative party as it was enunciated by its great leader, I subscribe.
In the course of this debate the statement was made that we have in this country two official languages but that Canada was not a bilingual country, and to that statement the Minister of Justice, and I think one other hon. member, took exception. I submit to you. sir, and this house, that the statement is absolutely accurate. When Canada was ceded to England in 1763 by the Treaty of Paris, Canada became a crown colony of England, and by virtue thereof English inherently for all purposes was an official language in this country. I shall not stop to outline the changes which came about by the Constitutional Act of 1791 and the Act of Union of 1840, but shall content myself with pointing out that by the constitution of this country, the British North America Act, by section 133 French was made an official language, an official language for all purposes prescribed by section 133 of that act, and with the limitations therein set out. Therefore, sir, I say to you that because the French language is limited and prescribed by section 133 of the British North America Act, Canada is not a bilingual country in the sense that both languages are official on exactly the same basis, and therefore there should be no room for objection to the statement which was made.
Another word was used, I think quite properly, to which apparently great exception was taken, namely the word "concession." When for any reason this parliament should see fit, either by its own substantive legislation or by request for amendment of the British North America Act, to extend the official use of the French language in this country, then I say that is a concession. Anything which confers a new right or an extended right upon the use of the French language in this country is a concession, and
I submit that the word is a perfectly proper one to use and is not in the least offensive.
The minister, referring to this section 15, said that the matter was a very simple one, and he went on to outline the reason why. To me, in a way, the matter is a very simple one, and yet fortunately or unfortunately we seem to approach it from a quite different viewpoint, and our convictions in some respects seem to be diametrically opposed. The Minister of Justice proceeded to argue that prior to the enactment of the Bank of Canada Act the commercial banks had the right to issue notes or bills in the French language, the English language, or in French and English, and because by a process under the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act, the issuing authority becomes in time solely the Bank of Canada, therefore a right was being taken away from the French people.
I should like to point out that for many years the Dominion of Canada issued bills which were legal tender. The Minister of Justice gave an instance of a French-speaking man desiring to make legal tender, or to place money in court, and he could not obtain a bill in French which was legal tender with which to make that deposit. May I point out to my hon. friend that from confederation down to the date of the passing of the Bank of Canada Act in 1934, Canada printed one and two dollar bills, five hundred dollar bills and one thousand dollar bills, and one or two other denominations, which were the only legal tender in this country. Those bills were printed solely and only in the English language.
Speaking in regard to the same matter, my hon. friend said: We-and I assume he meant by that the French people of this country-are not conceded the right to live or to breathe the air of this country. I realize that that sentence was a metaphorical one, but it implied that this parliament or the Englishspeaking people of this country were attempting to take away from their French-speaking fellow-citizens some right which they now have. I want to point out that no attempt is being made to take away any right to the use of the French language as guaranteed by the British North America Act or any other act upon our statute books. We who resist merely say to you who are represented by the words of the minister, that the minority in this country shall not prescribe by law the kind of air which the majority are to breathe. I do not claim any right or privilege to speak for the majority of people in this countrj', but I do claim the right or privilege to speak for hundreds of thousands of people who have a viewpoint which I am going to endeavour to outline.

May I come back again for a moment to the word "concessions"? In 1934 when the central bank was formed there was-I hope this word will not be offensive but I use it for want of a better one-an agitation for bilingual currency. The arguments advanced at that time were that the French people in this dominion had been able to get notes in their own language from the commercial banks and, therefore, the bills of the new central bank should be printed in French. The same argument is advanced to-day by the Minister of Justice. The government of that day, in a spirit of compromise and out of consideration for our French-speaking fellow-Canadians, enacted that the central bank bills should be printed both in French and in English so that the citizens of this country could have a choice. To-day the very fact that that concession was granted is used as one of the strongest arguments why this parliament should provide for bilingual bills.
Nothing more clearly illustrates or justifies the viewpoint of so many English-speaking people in this country than the illustration I have just given, that the French speaking people are constantly on the aggressive to force on the English-speaking people the French language.	,

I wish to say just a few words. I shall not take up much of the time of the house because it is getting near the end of the session and I have never yet been guilty of taking up more time than necessary. I wish to congratulate the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Lawson) upon his well reasoned argument against bilingual money. His speech was moderate and he handled the subject very capably. I endorse his views and am behind them. I am sorry I did not hear the address of my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) the other night, which I am told was a very good one, nor did I hear the speech, in supposedly moderate tones, of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on that occasion. I was not in the house at the time. I did, however, note his tone this afternoon, and it was not as moderate as I should have expected from a man of his type. He talks about racial unity but what he preaches in this regard he does not practise very much, especially at election time in the province of Quebec. I do not believe that hon. gentlemen from Quebec are expressing the views of the innocent, good-thinking people of that province, any more than the Progressives in this house, when there were sixty-five of them, expressed the views of the people when they talked secession and advocated getting out of confederation. They were not at that time expressing the views of the west any more than the French-speaking members in this house express the views of the good French
people of the province of Quebec. The trouble is that a few of the more educated people of Quebec, like the Minister of Justice and others, poison the minds of the innocent people of that province against our party, and there is always a war somewhere to create trouble and friction.
No one appreciates more than I do the hospitality of the French people; I have been among them and have been entertained by them in Montreal. Anything that I say now is rather more in their interests than in those of my own race in Ontario. I hate an argument of this kind, and while I do not know very much English and still less French I do know, from my experience in the business world and in this house, that a debate of this sort will create friction and result in lack of harmony in the country. I remember that on one occasion an hon. gentleman from the province of Quebec moved a resolution which I knew at the time would cause friction, and I appealed to him to withdraw it. I believe it was the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) who offered a resolution to the effect that no one but a bilinguist should hold a position in the civil service. What would that mean? It would mean that only someone who could speak French as well as English could get a job in the civil service. As far as I am concerned, there are two classes of people I shall not grant concessions to; the French are one, unless they make some concessions to us, because we want to be fair to them.
I do not want to take up the time of the house but I am utterly opposed to the change proposed in this bill. I do not see any reason why this government should attempt to change everything that a sane and sensible government put through in the last five years. They have attempted to change the British North America Act, the railway trustees, and now they are changing the Bank of Canada Act, making a mess of the whole thing. I am speaking not from a political point of view but from long training in the business world, and along that line I know as much as the ministers do. I honestly believe that it would be well to withdraw the proposal contained in this bill and, as my hon. friend, the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) who sits behind me has suggested, to take it out of the house and forget it. It is simply creating friction and bad racial feeling in the country, and that will be the result of the whole matter. Let me say further that if this goes on much longer I can warn the people in Quebec that they will probably suffer more than the other provinces, because I assume they do not want to be isolated, and that is

Every time there was an election in the province of Quebec there was talk of a war somewhere, and men of a higher type and education polluted the minds of the French people to make them believe that the Conservative party was a warring party and that if they wanted their sons to go to war they should vote for the Conservative party. Do hon. members mean to tell me that is fair tactics; that it will create harmony and unity? I say no. We are having difficulties in Ontario and my hon. friends will create more difficulty between Ontario and Quebec. I say to them: If I were you I would change my tactics and play the game fairly so as to have unity in this country instead of disruption.
Let the hon. member over here who is laughing say just what he thinks. I do not believe I am saying anything out of the way. Everything I have stated is true, and I believe it absolutely. What the government is doing to-day is creating a lack of harmony which will never be suppressed, although the hon. minister put his case to the house in a very clever way. I am sorry I am not able to equal his performance. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) has also this afternoon delivered his address in a quiet and commendable way, entirely without bad feeling. He appealed for harmony, and I believe that is what we want. The same attitude was taken by

the hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I have no ill feeling whatever against the French language; all I wish to say is: Please do not continue to ask concession after concession and never be satisfied.

-and it will not be a bilingual note. I inveighed against the government when the Bank of Canada Act was first brought up. I did so, not on the question of bilingualism but because of the action of the government as to taking control of the shares of the bank, involving an expenditure of $5,100,000 to secure 51 per cent of the shares, when the same amount of money should have controlled the whole of the shares. The days that have passed have made me none the easier in my mind about the activity of the government in this respect. I find that practically all the provinces in their companies' acts permit the shareholder, when an enlargement of the capital is brought about, to have the first opportunity of obtaining pro rata of their share holdings in the new capital. The Dominion Bank Act, section 32 reads thus:
The capital stock of the bank may be increased from time to time, by such percentage, or by such amount, as is determined upon by by-law passed by the shareholders at the annual general meeting, or at any special general meeting called for the purpose.
Section 33 contains the following:
Any of the original unsubscribed capital stock, or of the increased stock of the bank, shall, at such time as the directors determine, be allotted to the then shareholders of the bank pro rata, at such price, not less than par, and on such terms as are fixed by the directors.
The Dominion Companies Act states:
The directors of the company may, at any time after fifty per centum of the authorized capital stock of the company has been subscribed and ten per centum of such subscribed stock has been paid in, make a by-law for increasing the capital stock of the company to any amount which they consider requisite for the due carrying out of the objects of the company.	.
No by-law for increasing the capital stock of the company, or for subdividing the shares, shall have any force or effect whatsoever, until it is sanctioned by at least two-thirds of the votes cast at a special general meeting of the shareholders of the company duly called for considering the same, and afterwards confirmed by supplementary letters patent.
So that, throughout the whole of the procedure of the government in these matters as it allows companies and individuals to express themselves, it has been conceded that

Bank of Canada-Mr. Bennett
existing shareholders have a right to take their pro rata holdings in any increase of capital. And again I inveigh against the government for their attitude in this regard. There is neither excuse nor reason for what they have done, and for that reason I was entirely prepared to vote against the bill.
But, Mr. Speaker, a much larger issue has been raised, and I find myself thrown high and dry, having been tossed about by the progress of this debate. I have tried to see this matter reasonably and broadly, and I have come to the conclusion that the only view to take is not necessarily the broad view but the long view. We are a country in progress. AVe are a country with two languages. We have two sets of ideas. We have two hopes; we are attempting to merge them. I can quite understand the desire of the French people to begin this merger by infusing themselves into the general purpose of our progress. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) spoke of the progress in South Africa, where, he said, approximately 51 per cent of the people spoke the two languages. He is talking of to-day, but he is not talking of the period after the Boer war. The situation has been entirely reversed, although in certain sections of the country I have heard the youth talking together very freely and using words, from both languages, so intermixed that one was puzzled to know whether the individuals talking were Dutchmen or Englishmen. The same thing will obtain in Canada if we can permit the proper fusion of the two races. But as long as we are kept apart by racial distinctions and racial ideas, and by little differences developed and engendered, we shall never produce in this dominion a true homogeneous nation.
For that reason I am in direct sympathy with this bill and, taking the two questions together, the one on which I feel very strongly the government has done wrong, and the other one on which I feel very strongly the government is unconsciously moving in the right direction, I feel compelled to say that I shall vote with the government on the question of this bill.
