I had hoped to be spared further participation in this debate, but in view of the observations this afternoon of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the use of the word "bigotry" and other words equally offensive, I am compelled to make a few remarks. I indicated a few days ago that I speak only my own opinion and my own mind. I have not suggested to those associated with me that they should 12739-240
follow my course, but, holding certain convictions and believing as I do that the course taken by the previous administration is the one best calculated to advance the cause of amity and good will in Canada, knowing something as I do of the history of this country with respect to these matters, I urged as strongly, as dispassionately and as moderately as I could that the government give a longer period of time within which to ascertain whether the measures which were adopted in 1934, and which did not become effective for some months thereafter, were not those which in practice would be found satisfactory. I agree with what has been said by many members who have spoken in this house that we have a common purpose, a desire to create a homogeneous country, a desire out of diverse elements to produce a common nationality, a desire to make the name Canadian on this northern half of the north American continent representative of a personality, a nationality, a people. That can be done only by the union in spirit and in deed, in act and in purpose, of men and women of all nationalities.
When a few days ago the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) referred to the words of the late Sir John A. Macdonald, dealing with a matter to which I shall have to refer before I take my seat, the hon. gentleman quoted Sir John as saying that in this country there was no conquered people. Why, certainly that is true, Mr. Speaker. We have had generations come and go since 1759 and it would indeed be strange if in 1890, when Sir John was speaking, there should be any people that would refer to any other people in this country as a conquered people. Sir John said that since 1867 we had been British people, living under the protecting aegis of the British flag, as one dominion, and in that sense and1 in that regard what he said then is true to-day.
But, sir, there is something that we cannot forget, and it is that the facts of history endure. Not heaven itself can change the past. What has been, has been. There was a Treaty of Paris in 1763. There was a union of upper and lower Canada in 1840. There was an act of confederation in 1867. These are facts of history. They are not the notions of individuals; they are not things that can disappear because we wish to forget them. For good or ill they are the facts of history, just as other matters are facts of history. And as from all events in history there follow results, which we sometimes speak of as the implications of the events but which in the end are perhaps the controlling influences and factors in national life, so from these events to which I have referred there have flowed



Bank of Canada-Mr. Bennett
results which are embodied not only in the statutes of our country but in the very life of Canada itself.
Shortly after I accepted, at the hands of my party, its leadership, I went to Quebec. I travelled over large sections of that province. I addressed meetings in many parts of it, and no more kindly reception was ever given me than I received from my fellow-Canadian citizens in that province. And I told them, as frankly and as clearly as I could speak, that I realized the appeals which had been made to them. I realized, as the Minister of Justice so aptly said the other evening, that in that province there was a class who believed that there had been some sacrifice of their rights and that within the confederation they could not work out the destiny they had contemplated for themselves and their people. I told them then, as I say here and now from my place as a member of this house, that their constitutional rights, the laws, customs and practices of the constitution, would be respected by me at whatever cost it might involve to me personally. I called upon them and appealed to them to respect the constitution as a document which was arrived at after much consideration, much toil and much travail by the great public men of that time, and as indicative of what might constitute a fair relationship between the two great races.
I never hesitated, sir, to make that as clear as, by language, I could convey it to those who heard me, and when the results of the election were known we had in that province at least a fair su/pport. But no one could say that he had been elected by appeals made either to racial prejudices or to ancient animosities, to race or to religion, or upon other than the broad basis of those constitutional rights which are vouched for by a constitutional document and by that document guaranteed as the rights alike of minorities and majorities. And I have always regarded it as a matter of supreme satisfaction, Mr. Speaker, that the party to which I belong received from the electors of Quebec the measure of confidence which it did receive. I am not ignorant-because I do read the press of Quebec-of appeals that have been made looking toward, shall I say, the creation of another state, as the Minister of Justice said the other evening. I am not unmindful of that, but I agree with the hon. gentleman that it would be in the worst possible interests of those who would be affected that that should come about. And however much we may have cause to complain of the results of appeals that were made I have never complained, neither shall I to-day nor at any other time complain, of the result of

the appeal to the electors in the province of Quebec in 1935. It was a significant circumstance that it should happen as it did. I have overlooked, as part of the incident of party warfare, the appeals that were made about the war in Egypt in 1930, or the war in Turkey. I do not think that represents the genius or thought of great leaders, but it does represent the action which may be taken, in the heat of an election, by those to whom victory is their chief duty and supreme concern, to appeal to those passions and prejudices which are found at times beneath the skin of any man and every man, whether he be Anglo-Saxon or French.

Mr. Speaker, whatever
complaints may have been made with respect to the course which I followed in other parts of Canada with respect to other Canadians,

Bank oj Canada-Mr. Bennett
this at least will have to be admitted, that the position I took in the province of Quebec I took in every other province of confederation. At the outset of my leadership I made it clear that we would deal with all such problems on a national basis, because I realized that on more than one occasion the country had been tom asunder by what seemed to be small issues but which had most, shall I say, disastrous effects upon the efforts being made to build here a united Canada.
I wonder if bon. members of this chamber are aware of the fact that we have drawn our population in the western provinces from all quarters of the world. For instance, out of a total population, according to the last census, of 921,785 for the province of Saskatchewan, only 437,856 are of British origin. That in itself is reason why we should exercise the utmost care in dealing with problems of this kind. Aware of that fact, I fancy, as well as any other man in this country, and fully understanding the difficulty we were experiencing in welding into a harmonious whole the country west of the great lakes, to say nothing of the difficulties which obtained by reason of geographical conditions, I took the view that the constitution would be our guide. It has been the guide of the Conservative party since that date, and it was our guide during the days of Macdonald.
For instance, the other evening when the Minister of Justice was reading from the speech of Sir John A. Macdonald he might have gone further and read from that speech references Sir John made not only to conditions which then existed but to difficulties which he 'had experienced in his lifetime in dealing with this problem. Sir John had pointed out that he had met with opposition, and that to mould this country into a harmonious whole 'had been a most difficult task. After using the language to which the Minister of Justice referred the other evening, Sir John A. Macdonald used these words:
But while I say so much, Mr. Speaker, I must regret that my hon. friend, perhaps yielding to the necessity of his position as a party leader, should have commenced his speech with some party attacks against the Tories. My hon. friend felt constrained, I suppose, to make those allusions, which, in the circumstances of the case, I think were not altogether generous or altogether politic. The hon. gentleman spoke of the spirit of this bill being that of Toryism, utter Toryism, oppressive Toryism. Why, sir, if he looks at the history of England in modern days, I think he will find that most of the Liberal measures passed there have been passed, if not by Tories, by Conservatives. I think also, if he will look at the history of Canada, he will find at all events, that liberality towards the French-Canadian race was pretty much con-12734-240 i
fined to the Conservative party. The hon. gentleman had to admit that while this bill was, as he affirmed, an evidence of utter Toryism, the exclusion of the Franch language, the injury done to the French people, the insult offered to them, came from a radical, the Earl of Durham. To he sure, my hon. friend said that Lord Durham was a radical who did not understand all about liberty That is quite evident; and so great a radical was he that in order to get rid of him the English government sent him to this country to show us his Liberalism by attempting to deprive half the people of their right to use their own language. Ay, Mr. Speaker, and he succeeded in carrying out that effort; he succeeded in excluding the French language, and the measure was carried by a Liberal government in England. That was in 1840. The first government formed in Canada under that measure in 1841 was a confused government, where Liberals, and Tories, and officials were	mixed up	together.	But,	sir, in 1844when	there was	a stand-up	fight	between Conservatives and Liberals, when the Conservatives ralied around Lord Metcalfe, and carried a majority; when the parliament met in Montreal	in that	year, with a	Conservativemajority, the whole of the French-Canadian race,	with the	exception,	I think, of four,
were in opposition to the government. I was then elected for the first time, and I sat in that parliament as a Tory, a supporter of Lord Metcalfe. In that parliament the Freneh-Canadians were powerless; and yet, Mr. Speaker, what did that house do? Let me read to you a resolution that was passed, not by a Liberal or radical government, not by a parliament having sympathy with the French-Canadians exactly, but by a Conservative parliament elected, as was then alleged, in opposition to the interests of the province of Lower Canada; and yet passed, from a mere sense of justice, and without one single dissenting voice. Yes, from a mere sense of justice, the resolution was passed and the address was passed without one dissenting voice. I as a member of the young Tory party, was proud then to have the opportunity of pronouncing on that question. The yeas and nays were not taken because we were unanimous, but I was proud of having had a part, as a member of a great party, in the resolve to relieve our French-Canadian friends from the oppressive action of the Liberal government in England, at the instigation of the radical Earl Durham.
Then he quoted the address. From that day to this those who are familiar with the political history of Canada will have to admit that the position taken by the Conservative party has been consistent with the policy then outlined by Sir John A. Macdonald. It will be remembered that when confederation became an accomplished fact it followed two sets of resolutions, the London resolutions agreed to in, 1866 and the Quebec resolutions agreed to in 1864. It is pertinent to keep in mind what those resolutions were, for when discussion took place as to what should be done with respect to language it will be remembered that that question was dealt with, and it will be with-

Bank of Canada-Mr. Bennett
in the memory of every hon. member familiar with the subject that in the resolution finally arrived at in 1864 these words appear as the forty-sixth of the Quebec resolutions agreed to on October 10, 1864:
Both the English and French languages may be employed in the general parliament and in its proceedings, and in the local legislature of lower Canada, and also in the federal courts and in the courts of lower Canada.
When the London conference was held, resolution No. 45 was passed reading as follows:
Both the English and French languages may be employed in the general parliament and in its proceedings, and in the local legislature of lower Canada, and also in the federal courts and in the courts of lower Canada.
When the British North America Act was drafted, after these resolutions had been laid before the colonial secretary of the day, the first set of resolutions having been signed by
E.	P. Tache, and the London resolutions having been signed by Sir George Cartier, it will be recalled that section 133 crystallized into legislative form the purport of these resolutions, and that is important to keep in mind because it has a direct bearing on everything that thereafter happened. Section 133 reads:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and m or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
In order to understand the full significance of that, it is important to recall what the situation was in 1840. I have referred to the Treaty of Paris of 1763, and after that the provision made by the parliament at Westminster for the government of Quebec need not be dwelt upon except to say that there were two provinces, upper and lower Canada, and in lower Canada you had one set of considerations, in upper Canada another.
But in 1840 we find that an enactment was passed which prohibited the further use of the French language in the united provinces, and I shall, in order that the record may be complete, point out and read what that provision was;
And be it enacted that from and after the said reunion of the said two provinces, all writs, proclamations, instruments for summoning and calling together the legislative council and legislative assembly of the province of Canada and for proroguing and dissolving the

same, and all writs of summons and election, and all writs and public instruments whatsoever relating to the said legislative council and legislative assembly or either of them, and all returns to such writs and instruments, and all journals, entries, and written or printed proceedings of what nature soever of the said legislative council and legislative assembly and each of them respectively, and all written or printed proceedings and reports of committees of the said legislative council and legislative assembly respectively, shall be in the English language only:	Provided always, that this
enactment shall not be construed to prevent translated copies of any such documents being made, but no such copy shall be kept among the records of the legislative council or legislative assembly, or be deemed in any ease to have the force of an original record.
That was the statute passed by the parliament at Westminster in 1840, and the incident to which Sir John A. Macdonald referred was the passing of the resolution that brought about the end of that condition. That was not, however, until 1848, so that from 1840 to 1848 the united provinces of upper and lower Canada were prohibited by law from using any language other than English, and translated copies of the records of proceedings in that legislature were not allowed to be kept as part of the official records. But in 1848 there was passed the Union Act Amendment Act, which provided:
Whereas by an act passed in the session of parliament held in the third and fourth years of Her Present Majesty, intituled "An act to reunite the provinces of upper and lower Canada, and for the government of Canada," it is amongst other things enacted that from and after the said reunion of the said two provinces, all writs, proclamations, instruments for summoning and calling together the legislative council and legislative assembly of the province of Canada, and for proroguing and dissolving the same, and all writs of summons and elections, and all writs and public instruments whatsoever relating to the said legislative council and legislative assembly, or either of them, and all returns to such writs and instruments, and all journals, entries, and written or printed proceedings, of what nature soever, of the said legislative council and legislative assembly, and of each of them respectively, and all written or printed proceedings and reports of committees of the said legislative council and legislative assembly respectively, shall be in the English language only: Provided always that the said enactment shall not be construed to prevent translated copies of any such documents being made, but no such copy should be kept among the records of the legislative council or legislative assembly, or be deemed in any case to have the force of an original record:
And whereas it is expedient to alter the law in this respect, in order that the legislature of the province of Canada, or the said legislative council and legislative assembly respectively, may have power to make such regulations herein as to them may seem advisable:
Be it therefore enacted by the Queen's most excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present parliament

Bank oj Canada-Mr. Bennett
assembled, and by the authority of the same, that from and after the passing of this act so much of the said recited act as is hereinbefore recited shall be repealed.
That was in 1848.

speechtext: Who was the mover?

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
It was an- act of the
imperial parliament. I have not the name of the member of that house who had the matter in hand, but it could easily be obtained from the library if the hon. gentleman wishes.
In 1848, which, as will be seen, was nineteen years before confederation, there was a repeal of the statute which provided that the English language only should be the language to be used in the legislature of upper and lower Canada. Then followed the conferences to bring about the union of Canada, the union of the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario, upper and lower Canada, and when they met together at Quebec in 1864 they passed the resolution to which I have referred embodying the views of the minority of that time as adequate for the defence of their rights. That was No. 46 of the Quebec resolutions passed in 1864. Then, when they went to London a few months later for the purpose of having .the statute enacted or passed by the imperial parliament, the resolution which I have just read, No. 45, was arrived at, and that was regarded in the minds of Sir George Cartier and other great French-Canadians of that day as being adequate for the protection of their rights, their liberties, their language and other matters to which I shall presently refer.
Then we come to confederation, and the British North America Act, with section 133 embodying the provisions of resolution No. 45 of the London conference and resolution No. 46 of the Quebec conference, and any students of history who are interested and will look at the personnel of that distinguished gathering which met at Quebec and enacted these resolutions will have no difficulty in realizing that our French-Cana-dian. citizens were ably represented there by men who reflected in every respect the genius of their race.
Then came the question of the consideration of this matter when Sir John A. Macdonald and those associated with him came back to Canada and asked the legislature to adopt confederation. At that time one of the very first questions suggested was one connected with language, and what do we find? We find that that question was raised by a distinguished Frenchman of his day who realized its importance and made no apology for having raised the issue. When section 133
was being referred to, the Hon. Mr. Evanturel -you will find this at page 943 of the Debates of Confederation-said:
I wish to put a question to the government. I acknowledge that if I confined myself to consulting my own ideas, I should not put this question; but I do so in order to meet the wishes of several of my friends, both within this house and beyond its precincts. Those friends have expressed alarm in relation to one of the causes of the resolutions, and have requested me to ask an explanation from the hon. attorney general for Upper Canada, as to the interpretation of that clause. I had therefore to ask him whether article 46 of the resolutions, which states that "both the English and French languages may be employed in the general parliament and in its proceedings, and in the local legislature of Lower Canada," is to be interpreted as placing the use of the two languages on an equal footing in the federal parliament? In stating the apprehensions entertained by certain persons on this subject -and I consider that it is a mark of patriotism on their part, and that their apprehensions may be legitimate-I hope the government will not impute to me any hostile intention, and will perceive that the course I adopt is in their interests, as it will give them an opportunity of dissipating the apprehensions in question.
That was approved by the house, for the words "hear, hear" appear after that statement. Sir John A. Macdonald then rose and said:
I have very great pleasure in answering the question put to me by my hon. friend from the county of Quebec. I may state that the meaning of one of the resolutions adopted by the conference is this, that the rights of the French Canadian members as to the status of their language in the federal legislature shall be precisely the same as they now are in the present legislature of Canada in every possible respect. I have still further pleasure in stating that the moment this was mentioned in conference, the members of the deputation from the lower provinces unanimously stated that it was right and just, and without one dissentient voice gave their adhesion to the reasonableness of the proposition that the status of the French language, as regards the procedure in parliament, the printing of measures, and everything of that kind, should be precisely the same as it is in this legislature.
After some further observation Mr. Dorion, later Sir Antoine, rose and said:
So that if, to-morrow, this legislature choose to vote that no other but the English language should be used in our proceedings, it might do so, and thereby forbid the use of the French language. There is, therefore, no guarantee for the continuance of the use of the language of the majority of the people of Lower Canada, but the will and the forbearance of the majority. And as the number of French members in the general legislature, under the proposed confederation null be proportionately much smaller than it is in the present legislature, this ought to make hon. members consider w-hat little chance there is for the continued use of their language in the federal legislature. This is the only observation I have to make on this subject, and it was suggested to me by the answer of the Hon. Attorney General West.
Bank of Canada-Mr. Bennett

The attorney general, Sir John A. Macdonald, then rose and said:
I desire to say that I agree with my_ hon. friend that as it stands just now the majority governs; but in order to cure this, it was agreed at the conference to embody the provision in the Imperial Act. (Hear, hear.) This was proposed by the Canadian government, for fear an accident might arise subsequently, and it was assented to by the deputation from each province that the use of the French language should form one of the principles upon which the confederation should be established, and that its use, as at present, should be guaranteed by the Imperial Act. (Hear, hear.)
Thereupon, near the close of the debate, Sir George Cartier rose and said:
I will add to what has been stated by the hon. Attorney General for Upper Canada, in reply to the hon. member for the county of Quebec and the hon. member for Hochelaga, that it was also necessary to protect the English minorities in Lower Canada with respect to the use of their language, because in the local parliament of Lower Canada the majority will be composed of French Canadians. The members of the conference were desirous that it should not be in the power of that majority to decree the abolition of the use of the English language in the local legislature of Lower Canada, any more than it will be in the power of the federal legislature to do so with respect to the French language. I will also add that the use of both languages will be secured in the Imperial Act to be based on these resolutions. (Hear, hear.)
I said a moment ago that this discussion took place during the debates on confederation; I should have said that it took place after the resolutions had been submitted to the legislature and before the statute had in fact been passed. I think I have made clear what the conditions were that led up to the enactment of the British North America Act. I trust I have made clear to every hon. member of this house the circumstances under which section 133 became part of the constitution of Canada. It was enacted by the imperial parliament in furtherance of the resolutions arrived at both at Quebec and at London. The meaning to be attributed to that section is the meaning which was agreed upon in the legislature when the debates took place, as indicated, by Sir John A. Macdonald, the Hon. Mr. Evanturel, the late Sir Antoine Dorion and lastly by Sir George Cartier. These are the circumstances which led up to the enactment of this provision.
We inquire logically: How has that been interpreted by successive governments in Canada? It must be recalled that during the early days of this confederation Sir John A. Macdonald was Prime Minister until 1873; he and his government had control of the destinies of Canada until that year. From

1873 to 1878 we had Mr. Mackenzie and from 1878 to 1891 we had Sir John A. Macdonald, with successive Conservative administrations until 1896. From 1896 to 1911 we had a Liberal administration under the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It therefore becomes pertinent, nay, essential, that we should inquire as to the construction which parliament has placed upon that provision. If we can, by reference to the records or to the statements of public men of representative administrations, arrive at conclusions, they will be a help and a guide to assist us in discharging difficult and similar obligations and duties.
First of all, we find that we were admitting new provinces to the confederation. Only three years had elapsed until the Manitoba Act was passed. This is a very important act as it provided the conditions that would obtain in Manitoba with respect to the use of language. It will be remembered that in the statute creating that province special provision was made for the use of the French language. Some of my hon. friends seem to be unaware of that fact. They do not seem to realize that the Manitoba Act as passed in 1870 contained this provision, which will be found in the constitutional documents of Canada at page 69, and which reads:
Either the English or the French language [DOT] may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the legislature, and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process, in or issuing from any court of Canada established under the British North America Act. 1867. or in or from all or any of the courts of the province. The acts of the legislature shall be printed and published in both those languages.
This was the constitutional legislation under which the Conservative government of that day brought the province of Manitoba into being. Bear in mind that that was in 1870, only three years after confederation became an actuality. This act was continued until circumstances to which I shall presently allude came into being.
The province of British Columbia was admitted into confederation in 1871, but no provision of a similar kind was included in its constitution. On the contrary, the address merely provided that the provisions of the British North America Act should prevail. That is all that may be said with respect to that. But an agitation grew up.in western Canada. Why? I shall not answer that question. In 1890 the legislature of Manitoba, under Liberal leadership, enacted a statute which reads as follows:
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the legislative assembly of the province of Manitoba, enacts as follows:

1.	Any statute or law to the contrary notwithstanding, the English language only shall be used in the records and journals of the house of assembly for the province of Manitoba, and in any pleadings or process in or issuing from any court in the province of Manitoba. The acts of the legislature of the province of Manitoba need only be printed and published in the English language.
2.	This act shall only apply so far as this legislature has jurisdiction so to enact, and shall come into force on the day it is assented to.
What followed?

speechtext: Have there not always been very grave doubts as to the validity of that statute?

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
I am not discussing that phase of the matter. I am merely giving the historical view of the exact facts. I desire to remove my observations as far as possible from political considerations and to recite the facts just as they are, leaving them to speak for themselves. That was in 1890. There grew up at once an agitation on behalf of the minority, who felt that they had been deprived of privileges and rights that had been taken from them, an agitation that this legislation should be disallowed. There were presented1 to the government of the day petitions signed by leading citizens and members of parliament, by the Archbishop of St. Boniface and others, but the Jaws were left to their operation, and that statute, for whatever it may be worth, is part of the law of Manitoba to-day. It is not my duty or my business to express any opinion as to its validity; I must content myself with merely saying that there it is as part of the statute law of that province. As I say, that was in 1890. I did not go west until 1897, but I still recall that even seven years after the passing of that statute there were agitations in various parts of the west with respect to that law. But it survived and it is still, for whatever it may be worth, a part of the statute law of the province of Manitoba.
I have already dealt with British Columbia. When the two new provinces came into being, with respect to the question of language it was merely provided that the provisions of the British North America Act should apply, and there it rested. But in the meantime it was, of course, to be expected that in this parliament there would be many questions raised and many debates promoted for the purpose of discussing the situation, and in 1890 a debate took place upon the introduction of a bill by the late Dalton McCarthy in which he provided that the grant of powers given the Northwest Territories in 1877, which
Bank oj Canada-Mr. Bennett
made provision for the use of both languages, should be maintained. Mr. McCarthy moved the first reading of a bill for the purpose of terminating those rights and privileges as defined in the act of 1877. It was at that time that there took place the debate to which the Minister of Justice referred the other evening, the debate in 1890. It was then that Sir John A. Macdonald made the observations to which the hon. gentleman referred, and those observations are as true and pertinent to-day as when Sir John Macdonald uttered them. There was no conquered race in 1890; there is none to-day. Successive generations have taken the place of the first generation that lived and had its being in the province of Quebec in 1763. But here we had, precipitated into the chamber in the old building, at the instance of Mr. McCarthy, a discussion with respect to language in the Northwest Territories. Finally, on the motion of Sir John Thompson, seconded by Sir Adolphe Chapleau, then Secretary of State, the matter was left to the choice of the people, the choice of the legislature, the choice of those who should take the place of the representatives of the people after the general election, freedom of choice, the right of self-determination. That was left, at the instance of Sir John Thompson, in his amendment, seconded by Sir Adolphe Chapleau, to the motion of Mr. McCarthy, as the proper determination of that issue; and those of us familiar with the history of Sir Adolphe Chap-Leau will not for a moment say that he had not a burning zeal for his countrymen and as great a desire to promote their fortunes and their interest as any man within the sound of my voice, no matter where he may come from. I repeat, that was in 1890.
We are all familiar with the difficulties that arose out of the so-called Manitoba school question; we all remember the passing by a Liberal administration of the school laws of Manitoba; we all recall the judgment of the privy council, and none of us can fail to remember that that court decided that the rights of minorities had been prejudicially affected. Nor will any deny that the Conservative party of that day staked its existence and lost upon fidelity to the constitution. What is more, so fair were the Canadian people in their attitude to that question that when the votes were counted it was found that ouside the province of Quebec the Conservative government had been maintained in its position. The majority of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, for a reason which need not now be discussed and which has never been explained, was a majority that depended upon the votes he

Bank oj Canada-Mr. Bennett
succeeded in obtaining at that time in the province of Quebec. That was the position in 1896.
Now let us see what interpretation was placed upon the provisions of this law by others after that. We have, for instance, what was referred to this afternoon, and which seems to me to be fairly important. We have a question asked by Mr. Paquet on May 31, 1905, of the government of the day, presided over by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Minister of Finance of which was William Stevens Fielding, one of his most trusted lieutenants. I direct the attention of this chamber carefully to the words of the questions and answers given. Remember, I am giving a chronological record, and this was in 1905. The questions put to the government were these:
1.	Do any grave reasons of state exist that might prevent the Minister of Finance from having the dominion one and two dollar notes or all other bank notes printed simultaneously in English and French?
2.	Are they unaware in the Finance department that the two languages are official in Canada
3.	Is it the intention of the Minister of Finance to rectify in the future this state of things by ordering that those bank notes be printed in the both languages, English and French?
To that the Hon. W. S. Fielding, Minister of Finance, replied:
There is nothing in the British North America Act or in any act of the parliament of Canada which requires or contemplates the printing of dominion notes in two languages. The Finance department has not contemplated the advisability of any departure from the practice which has existed under all governments from the beginning of confederation down to the present time.
Those questions and those answers will be found at page 6826 of Hansard of May 31, 1905. May I pause for a moment to direct the attention of my fellow-members of this chamber to the significance of that language. It was not necessary for Mr. Fielding to use, speaking a9 he was for the administration, the exact words he did; he could have answered the question very simply. But instead of that he said:
There is nothing in the British North America Act or in any act of the parliament of Canada which requires or contemplates the printing of dominion notes in two languages.
That is a complete answer by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government to the position which has been taken in this chamber and elsewhere with respect to this matter. There is nothing under the constitution; there is nothing in any act of parliament that either contemplates or provides for the printing of bank notes in the two languages.

That is the answer made by Mr. Fielding. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, I am not for a moment putting my interpretation on- anything; I am merely reading the record as it is chronologically. I am merely placing on Hansard my answer to the charge of bigotry hurled at me this afternoon by the Prime Minister of Canada. There are the questions and there are the answers. There is the interpretation of the constitution given directly in- answer to questions which, as I say, need not have been answered in these terms but which were answered in the terms I have indicated.
But the matter did not end there. Obviously it would not. Those of us who knew the late Armand LaVergne and know Mr. Bourassa realized that in 1905 and years following, when they were members of this parliament, such a question would ultimately be raised. So a few years later the question was raised in this parliament. It was in 1905 that Mr. Fielding dealt with it as I have indicated. In 1907 the matter was again brought to the attention of parliament, and members of this house have referred to the matter on more than one occasion. In Hansard of that session, volume 2, there is a record of the discussion. The then hon. member for Nicolet, Mr. Devlin, had formerly been a member of the imperial House of Commons. Many of us in this chamber remember him; he was here when I came to the house in 1911. He referred to the fact that outside the British House of Commons speeches were not infrequently made in Welsh. He did not say so, but the fact is that speeches north of the Tweed are sometimes made in Gaelic.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Certainly, why not? And Mr. Devlin was referring to that fact.

A sign of universal
culture.

speechtext:
He then said, speaking of Canada-and I quote his words because he was a very precise gentleman:
Here the French language is official and recognized by all; consequently there is no occasion to fight in order to ensure its recognition.

Bank of Canada-Mr. Bennett
That is on page 3653 of Hansard of 1907. It became essential, of course, that the leader of the government, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, should speak upon the question. Sir Wilfrid did not deliver a lengthy speech, but he dealt with this very issue, and in language that indicates clearly the interpretation which he placed upon the constitutional powers which had been conferred upon his fellow-citizens and upon the parliament of Canada. On February 25, as reported at page 3655 of Hansard of 1907, he used these words:
But to affirm, as he does, that the French language should be used upon every occasion, and that every public document should be printed on one side in French and the other side in English, is, I think, going a little too far. For instance, I understand that my hon. friend wants bank notes to be printed either in French or in English. For my part I never yet saw an occasion where a bank note printed in English was not properly understood by the French people; and I am quite sure that a bank note printed in French "would be understood by the English people to be exactly what it means. But I see no reason why a bank note should not be printed in French. Since we have been in office we have not had occasion to issue a new form of bank notes, we have taken the old form as we found it, we have continued the form of the old bank notes. I do not see any reason why, if we were to issue a new form, we should issue it in one language rather than another. But I would say to my hon. friend that it is far better that we should be conservative in these matters and not to change our forms every now and then. We should keep the old form when it contributes towards security and public convenience, and when it is well understood. I do not think there has been any change in the form of the English hank note for over a hundred years.
At the close of his speech, when he moved the amendment to which reference was made this afternoon, he used these words:
But to come back to what I have already said, I do not insist for my part that the French language should be written and spoken everywhere. It is "not necessary to use French where every one understands English. But obviously the French should be used when it is more convenient for the people. So far I am disposed to agree with my hon. friend. But I must protest against the idea that because bank notes are not printed in French as well as English, the French language is not on a footing of equality with the English.
That was in 1907, only four years before Sir Wilfrid Laurier went out of office. In the meantime the discussions had assumed a far wider range than was originally intended, and had spread to many parts of the country. I do not think for a moment that as a result of those discussions there was, outside of Quebec, any manifestation of a desire that the bank notes should be printed in French as well as in English. But as far as I can understand the matter, at that time there
was no discussion in parliament at any great length, although the issue was raised incidentally on two or three other occasions.
There was an administrative matter that had to be dealt with, and the other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) referred to the election of 1930 and left the impression that he had heard his opponent make the statement that certain changes would take place in connection with the issue of money orders and postal notes. I have not received full details, but I am advised that the hon. gentleman and his opponent were never in a joint meeting during the campaign, and Mr. Turnbull says that no such language was used by him. What is more, he has written the Minister of Finance to that effect.

I now deal with the administrative side of the post office, for I had occasion carefully to consider it during my term of office. The word "postes" first appeared upon Canadian postal stamps in 1927. It was on the historical and pictorial issues, and dad not at that time have on it the engraving of the king's head. There were various engraved scenes. One was the fathers of confederation; another was the parliament buildings; there was one of Macdonald, one of Laurier, and one with a map of Canada. I took the trouble to satisfy myself as to when that first appeared upon a postage stamp. My information was that it was about the twenty-ninth day of June, 1927. Then came the question of the word appearing upon a postage stamp that carried the king's head. That first appeared on October 17, 1928. It was a green two cent stamp. The remainder were issued at a subsequent date. Then we had the great tercentenary stamps of 1908, which as a matter of courtesy were issued entirely in French. Now we come to the question of postal cards, post-cards so-called. The first bilingual post-cards were issued in January, 1912. It was a general issue. Protests came into the department of the Postmaster General from English provinces, and on December 16, 1917, Mr. Lemaire, who was then superintendent of the postal branch, on the authority of the Postmaster General, then Doctor Coulter, instructed that from December 17, 1917, bilingual cards were to be issued to Quebec and well known French communities elsewhere, and the others were to be in English. Then in the office at Ottawa bilingual post-cards were sold. Certain protests were made in 1919 and as a result we had a change by which, following the general practice, from 1923 on offices were divided into three classes, English, French and bilingual. To the English offices only English supplies were supposed to be sent; to the French offices French supplies were to be sent, and where there was a mixed population of English and French supplies in each language were sent in such proportions as were regarded as necessary to meet the requirements which might arise.

I am bound to say, Mr. Speaker, that I believe that system worked out satisfactorily, because it is still in effect. My inquiries a few months ago led me to believe-and I take it to be so yet-that as new offices came into being they were classified either as English, French or bilingual, and the supplies were dealt with accordingly. That is hardly true, however, with respect to money orders. Money orders are in international use, which obviates the necessity of having them printed separately in the two languages. Bilingual money orders have been in use and are in use at present; they have been bilingual in Quebec since 1881 and generally since the first day of July, 1882. Postal notes for domestic circulation have been bilingual since 1906, when they were introduced. As far as forms are concerned, they have been dealt with in the manner I have indicated, English for the English, French for the French, bilingual for communities where there were both French and English. Unfortunately, however-and at one time I was not sure that it was not done with purpose-sometimes French forms were circulated in English offices, and there was much trouble. Sometimes English forms were sent to French offices, and there was trouble; sometimes only English or French forms were circulated to offices listed as bilingual. Great difficulties were experienced, which caused much trouble. Letters were written to the newspapers, and matters of that sort. _
That is the sort of thing which creates more disharmony than almost anything else of which I 'have knowledge. That sounds like a very small' thing, yet in my mail to-day I received a letter from Toronto complaining of the fact that the notices enclosed, both in French, had been sent from Montreal to a Toronto merchant with respect to a communication which had been dealt with by the district office. That is a plain blunder, but that is one of the difficulties which make for disharmony. That is one of the things which have brought about a great deal of this unfortunate discussion. Someone has blundered. On more than one occasion while I was in office in this country I took the opportunity to impress upon our friends who were responsible for distribution that they should try to see that no such mistake occurred. I recall vividly a protest from a Scotsman residing in an outlying section who went to his office, one in which there were no French-speaking people, and received a communication in French. He was very much annoyed about it, and he made a great deal of noise about it. That is the sort of thing

Bank oj Canada-Mr. Bennett
which should be prevented. That is that sort of thing which brings about the very difficulties to which I have alluded. Take the question of signs on post offices. They never have been welded together as one sign. There has been one sign "Post Office" and another "Bureau de Poste." The two signs have been used in bilingual offices, the French sign only in French offices and the English sign only in English offices. One of the difficulties that has arisen has been -brought about by some officious person trying to see what could be done, I sometimes think, to make trouble, taking one of the French signs into an English community and putting it up on the post office. That has created difficulty; that has brought about trouble. I say, Mr. Speaker, that at times I almost felt that this was done purposely, but of course I could not say it was because there was no evidence to that effect. Undoubtedly, however, it is these small things that have been conducive to preventing the harmony, shall I say, that otherwise should and would exist. The general effort of the Post Office Department has been to regulate as far as possible the distribution of supplies in order to prevent such occurrences, and I think it behooves every member of this house to use his or her influence to the uttermost to ensure, if -possible, that accidents such as these will not happen. They look small, I repeat; they seem insignificant, but, as has been pointed out in parliament on more than one occasion, such accidents have been the cause of much difficulty.
That was the condition with respect to administration in connection with the post office. There was an effort made to maintain the principle which was the foundation of the whole position, that there should be freedom of choice. That is, in the communities which were entirely French, on the basis of equality with their English-speaking fellow-Canadians they should have in their offices these forms and documents in their own tongue; the English should -have their documents in their tongue, and in communities where there were both French and English they should have bilingual forms or documents. That, at least, has been the aim on the part of the post office authorities. Other branches of the public service were dealt with in the same way.
When Sir Wilfrid Laurier was speaking in 1907 he referred to the fact that we had bills printed in English and in French. He did not think it desirable or necessary that they should be printed in English on one side and in French on the other. I pointed out
previously, as I do again, that the orders of the day, the bills and the proceedings of this house are open to the choice of the members of this chamber. A member can select whatever form he or she desires, an English form, a French form, a bill in the French language, a bill in the English language, the orders of the day in one language or the other. That is freedom of choice, of selection. That is the right that both Prime Ministers in days gone by, Sir John A. Macdonald, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, felt to be the proper way to deal with these problems so far as these conditions were concerned.
In 1934 we introduced into this parliament a bill dealing with a central bank, the Bank of Canada. That bill contemplated the creation of a bank which ultimately would be the only bank of issue. That is, by 1940,
I think it is, the major part of the notes circulating in this country will be notes of the Bank of Canada. There will still be notes of the chartered- banks circulating in Canada, but the bill provided, as the Minister of Justice pointed out, that these Bank of Canada notes should be legal tender, and there were other considerations which induced the then government to apply the principle that had been applied since 1867 and to afford to our fellow-citizens of French-Canadian origin an opportunity to obtain from the Bank of Canada notes printed and engraved in the French language. The statute provided that the Bank of Canada was always to have in stock, on hand, bills in both English and French so that they might be available as required. The vital words were "as required"; they should be there as required. They might not be required west of the lakes; they might be required only in small quantities or in small numbers. They might not be required to any great extent in the maritime provinces. They might be required in large numbers in New Brunswick, and very few might be required in Nova Scotia. They might be required in limited numbers in Prince Edward Island. But every branch of the Bank of Canada was in a position to meet the demands which would be made upon that bank for notes either in English or in French, as might be required. I repeat: The vital words were "as required."
I say that nothing could have been a fairer approximation to even-handed justice, as we proceeded with the interpretation of section 133 and other sections, bearing in mind what was said by Mr. Fielding, -than to accord- and I use the word "accord" out of deference to the statement of my hon. friend-to our fellow-citizens of French origin the right to

require notes of the Bank of Canada printed or engraved in the French language.
The Minister of Justice did not like my use of the word "concession." I did not use the word in any offensive sense; I used it in the sense in which one says, "I concede that point" or "I concede a point." And the parliament of Canada conceded the request that there should be afforded to fellow-Canadian citizens of French origin the right to obtain notes of the Bank of Canada engraved in the French language. That was conceding a point, and it was not using the word "concession" in any different sense from that of the word "forbearance" was used by Sir Antoine Dorion when he was discussing a question as to what might happen. The word was used not for the purpose of giving offence to the hon. member, but rather for the purpose of indicating that the government of the day was prepared to ask the parliament of Canada to concede the point. The point was the request that our fellow-Canadian citizens of French origin should be able, as required, to obtain notes printed or engraved in the French language.
The government of to-day takes the view that that should be ended. It has had but a short time in which to be tried. It was a distinct advance over the attitude taken by Mr. Fielding and it went even beyond the contemplations of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Certainly it was the greatest advance, so far as my hon. friends of French-Canadian origin are concerned, that had been made in Canada. For, as required, it gave them the right to receive from the Bank of Canada, or through the banks to receive from the Bank of Canada bills of that bank engraved in the French language.
The government of to-day through its Prime Minister and Minister of Justice says, "We have here a great majority; we represent a majority of the people of Canada; representing a majority of the people of Canada we propose to change all this and make a bilingual bill." I endeavoured to indicate what happened in western Canada in 1890, and in view of what has happened in this parliament the date is significant. I indicated what had happened with relation to the constitutional provision of the Manitoba Act of 1870, and I indicated, without repeating to-night what I said a few days ago, the protests that were made against the postal cards when they were made bilingual, and the action taken to try to placate, if you will, that position, and to bring about improved and harmonious relations between the two great peoples in this dominion. Although Mr. Fielding took the view that we should still cling to our English notes; although the notes of the Dominion 
of Canada were legal tender, and had always been legal tender, and although the ones, twos, hundreds, fifties, and thousand dollar bills were legal tender and the medium of exchange and settlement between bank clearing houses-although all this was so, the government of 1934 took the view that we would meet the requirements of our fellow-Canadian citizens of French origin by providing them, through every branch of the Bank of Canada, with bills engraved and printed in the French language. We took the view that to bring about the change to which I have directed attention we would not arouse the resentment which had arisen, out of the use of bilingual post cards, from the English speaking provinces.
We took the view that we would take every step possible to prevent that, by making it possible for the English-speaking provinces and those of English-speaking origin, and others, to receive English notes or notes engraved or printed in English, on the one hand, as against the requirements of their neighbours who have their notes printed or engraved in French. I wonder whether hon. members realize that that was not an easy step for a government to take? There were those who were opposed to that action. Notwithstanding the answer given by Mr. Fielding, the government of the day believed -that it was desirable, in the interests of national solidarity and harmony between peoples, that we should provide those who were of French origin and extraction, if they so required- and so desired, with notes printed or engraved in their language. It was the language of their childhood, the language they learned at their mothers' knees, and to meet their wishes we took this step.
At this point I must make it clear that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice were not quite fair when they suggested what they did with respect to majorities and minorities. They know perfectly well that what I was dealing with was the question of the majority of the population of this country being of British descent and the minority being of French descent, -and that it is an axiom that where the will of the minority is imposed upon the majority, except by invitation, acquiescence or the assistance of that majority, the result has always been disharmony. There has been no exception to that. The evidence of history, whether we take that of Europe or other parts of the world, has indicated the truth of that statement, and wdien there is the evidence that we have as to the resentment of the majority in the English provinces against bilingual post-cards in the manner

I say that I yield in a sense of tolerance to no man in this house, but I arrive at conclusions from carefully analyzing the history of my country. When in 1934 we arrived at the conclusion that we should take the step we did, we believed that to impose the will of this parliament upon the majority of those who live west of the lakes would be fraught with the greatest danger to harmony and good will and to peaceful contacts between peoples in the development of Canada. I have tried to make that as clear as I can because it represents my considered personal opinion, but I have not endeavoured' to press my opinion upon others. I have endeavoured in moderate' terms, as contrasted with the words of abuse that were hurled at us to-day, to present the case historically as it is, chronologically as it is, and to ask the members of this house to vote accordingly. It is no good to ask because it is well foreseen what the result of the vote will be. But I place before them the position as it is, and each one in his own conscience must answer whether or not in a community that is overwhelmingly British the circulation of notes of that kind is not fraught with the gravest danger to harmony between races in other parts of Canada. In the very nature of things, as the agitation proceeds, it will grow as it did in 1890,, and I wonder whether anyone would like to see again the conditions that were apparent in western Canada from 1S96 to 1900. And remember, although the Conservative party risked its existence by remaining true to the constitution, it lost, but it has never had any regrets for having done so. I have never had any regrets for supporting the party in 1896 in the views which it took. I was a very young man then, and I supported the party because I believed that the best assurance of peaceful relations between the descendants of the two great races in this country is to be found in each giving to the other Ithe least possible cause for offence. That is what I said. I use the word "offence" in no narrow sense. I could not help thinking, as I reviewed these matters in my own mind, as most other men have too, no doubt, of that great saying. "Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth." subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that it is to be regretted profoundly that such an agitation has been created in this parliament on such a question. It leads one to believe that in reality we have not been making very much progress towards a better understanding among
the nations of the world when we have such a discussion in the parliament of a nation ol only nine million population. I find it strange that the distinguished gentleman who leads the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has found it necessary to make a second speech on this question. With all due respect to him and with all the profound consideration that I have for his personality, I do not believe he improved what he said the other day and I do not think he has said anything which would justify the position he has taken.
For an hour and a half he has entertained the House of Commons on the lack of authority that this government has to propose such legislation. He gave us a lecture on what was said by the framers of the constitution. He read extracts from the resolutions which preceded confederation. He did all this to establish the fact that we have no right to do what he himself did in 1934. If we are not entitled to French or bilingual notes, I ask my right hon. friend what his justification was for introducing the legislation he introduced in 1934 to provide for two issues of notes, one in French and one in English.
Reference has been made to the last election campaign. During that campaign we were told by supporters of the right hon. gentleman that what he had done for the French-Canadian was much greater than what had been done by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the members of the Liberal government in general. Those who were candidates in the last election or who followed the campaign in the province of Quebec know that my right hon. friend and his ministers proclaimed all over that territory that he had gone to a much greater length than any Liberal government would have gone. We are now informed by the right hon. gentleman that he did less and that it was intended to be less than what was proposed by the Liberals in 1934.
I do not like hearing my right hon. friend say that upon such things as forms issued in French by the Post Office Department depend the harmony of Canada. If the harmony which exists to-day among all the citizens of our country is not strong enough to stand the issuing of French forms by the Post Office Department in place of an English form, then it is not worth while being preserved.
It may be true that under the strict letter of the law we cannot claim this right, but in all British countries and in all British institutions there has always been something besides the strict interpretation of the law. Usages and customs many times change the cold letter of the law. It is the history of British institutions that the dead letter of the law has been modified or been given some life
Hank oj Canada-Mr. Cardin

by usage and practices which have developed in parliaments as well as in other institutions in the British empire. It has been said that a concession has been made to the French people of Canada; the right hon. gentleman has said that he made a concession in 1934 when he authorized the printing of bills in French as well as in English. Even if it was a concession, even if it was a generous concession that he made at that time, are we not entitled to-day, by reason of our contribution to the life of Canada in what we have been trying to do to help to develop this country and to bring harmony, peace and good will among the Canadian people, to some recognition and to see occasionally the concessions granted- us enlarged to some extent with a view to fostering a greater feeling of understanding among Canadian citizens? Even if it was a concession, I say that we were entitled to that concession; and when we speak here of such concessions I would only ask my English-speaking fellow-countrymen to pay a visit some time to the province of Quebec where they will see what the word "concession" means. They will see there how the minority of the province of Quebec has been treated by the French majority. There is no question such as this one being raised in Quebec on any issue; we are ready to cooperate with our English-speaking fellow-citizens of that province, and there is no question of limiting the rights of minorities, no question of trying to promote harmony through the curtailment of rights, no question of trying to promote harmony through the diminution of initiative. We are making concessions in that province and greater concessions than we are asking the parliament of Canada to grant in favour of the French in this country. One has only to read the history of Canada to be convinced of the concessions that we have been making and are still making. Forms printed in French may be sent accidentally to English sections of the country, but forms are printed in both languages. I may say that in Quebec we have had and still have high officers of the federal government who do not speak a word of French but who have to deal with the French population of that province. There is a greater limitation of our rights than is involved in the issue of a form in one language. We have stood for that condition for a number of years and we are still standing for it, not asking for the dismissal of Englishspeaking superior officers in all departments in the province of Quebec, officers who do not speak the French language. We are doing our part to bring about a better under-
standing among all the citizens of Canada, and I cannot believe that a bilingual note of the Bank of Canada is going to disturb the harmony which now exists. If we were to follow the law as it is at present and issue French notes, these notes would be legal tender and would have circulation in Ontario, and they would have to be accepted as legal tender by Ontario and by the provinces of the west. Is it a greater insult to have a bilingual bill presented to creditors in Ontario than to have entirely French bills given them, as might happen if we left the law as it stands now? '
There is no danger of destroying the harmony that has existed among Canadian citizens. I had thought that our country was big enough to enable us to think of something else and to forget the small differences which have caused us so many difficulties in the past. I had thought that those difficulties had been removed and that there had grown up a better understanding of the points of view and the dispositions of the different sections of the country. Can we not in this year of grace 1936 look upon these problems in the British frame of mind instead of carrying into practice the old forgotten colonial spirit that existed long ago? I certainly thought the days of the colonial spirit had gone and we had reached a point where we could regard ourselves as all equal in this country without criticizing certain privileges, if you will, or certain concessions made to minorities. British institutions have been maintained throughout the world and England has kept its authority and power over the world not by restricting the liberties of people coming into the realm of the empire but by extending their liberties. The gospel of England has never been restriction, it has been the opposite, and it is by that bond of generosity and good will and the generous interpretation of statutes and treaties that England is to-day able to maintain its authority over so many countries in the civilized world. There are no races, no creeds, no colours in the British empire; there are human beings, whose well-being it has been the object of British institutions to further.
I hope that this little tempest will pass, and I sincerely regret that an amendment has been introduced at this stage of the legislation. The matter had been discussed very well in moderate terms by the leader of the opposition on the previous occasion. Why come forward on the third reading and raise a new issue, precipitating a full dress debate on this motion? As the leader of the opposition admitted, the bill is there and it is going to pass and become law because it is supported by the majority. It was supported on the

Bank oj Canada-Mr. MacNeil
second reading; it was supported in committee and after the third reading it will become law. Why then raise this issue by an amendment on the third reading? I hesitate to answer that question; with my limited knowledge of English I might incur the Speaker's displeasure. We should not look upon this country from the point of view of figures and numbers, from the point of view of majorities or minorities. We should look upon it as a whole and in that spirit which we are trying to foster in order to develop this wonderful land that is ours, the land called Canada. We should forget as much as possible the small difficulties of 1890. Let us forget the past; let the difficulties of 1890 be forgotten in 1936, when we are living in a new world. Let us forget all these small things and unite to bring about a better condition of things in Canada. We are fortunate enough to have in this country descendants of the two greatest races of the civilized world, the French and the English-speaking people of Canada. Let us be proud of that situation in which we are, and instead of fighting one another, instead of depriving one part of any of its privileges, if you will, or, if you prefer, of the concessions that have been made to it, let us unite in order to evoke the best that is in every one of our citizens, so that we may face the problems of the day and provide a greater measure of happiness for the people of Canada.
I am not ashamed of being of French descent; I do not propose to excuse myself for that. It is an accident of nature, which accident, I consider, is a happy one. I am as good a citizen as anyone who has been born a British subject, another accident of nature, and a happy one also. I have no apology to offer; I am here because my ancestors were here first. They were the first ones to open this country to civilization, the first ones who started to build up a big country in this new land. I wish to respect the laws of my country and the laws of the British empire. As a French-Canadian I have always been respectful of the laws under which we have been called upon by Providence to live. In the province of Quebec we have a law-abiding population, and we have done our share, with the gifts we got from old France, a country with which we have no connection to-day except for the mind and possibly for the heart; nationally speaking we have no connections with them. But we have inherited from that race certain gifts of which we are proud, and we are ready to apply them to the benefit of our country, to join with all other Canadian citizens to build up a happy and prosperous Canada. Let me ask in the name of harmony-not harmony through reduction 12739-241
of privileges, of concessions, or of advantages -that we work together in a spirit which will associate the gifts of the two races for the upbuilding of a better Canada. Let us forget, in these difficult times through which we are passing, our small differences; let us not be divided by small things.

Mr. Speaker, with many other members of this house I regret the general trend of this debate. I deplore any discussion at this time that may tend to accentuate racial differences or arouse racial prejudices. I have no political axe to grind; I have only a very earnest desire to stand shoulder to shoulder with my fellow countrymen who speak and love the French language in the advancement of the common welfare of all the Canadian people. I have very clearly in mind the war efforts of .our country in the years 1914 to 1918. In the Canadian corps there was no distinction in service or in sacrifice on the ground of racial origin. We were all Canadians; French-Canadians and English-Canadians alike gained a rare appreciation of each other's qualities, courage and loyalty, and there was achieved there a united effort in the service of the common cause which transcended other considerations and which in a large measure established in Canada a true national consciousness. I earnestly submit that at this time we should strive to attain that same spirit, that same tolerance, as we face our common problems in this dominion to-day.
An important suggestion was made this afternoon during the course of the debate in this house. The suggestion, which was made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), offers a satisfactory basis of compromise, and it conforms to the practice followed in other countries where they have bilingual difficulties. It enables the issue of a note which is in every sense of the word Canadian and which cannot by any manner or means offer offence to any citizen of this country. I propose to advance the suggestion by way of amendment. I feel that it offers members of this house an opportunity to evince the sincerity of their desire to maintain national harmony at this time. I move, therefore, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) an amendment to the amendment:
That there be added to the amendment the following words:
"and that there be substituted therefor a section to provide that the notes of the several denominations shall be in distinctive colours and designs and bear thereon no words other than ' Canada,' the appropriate numeral or numerals, the proper signatures, the serial number, and the year of issue."

They may succeed in defeating an odd Liberal government in Canada, but, after all, that is only an incident in the history of the Dominion of Canada. We have found from experience that it is an incident which the people of Canada remember for a long time because they are reminded of it every time they look at their tax bills for the next five or ten years afterwards. While they do remember such an experience for a considerable length of time afterwards, the one thing that we as a House of Commons and that parliament as a whole should remember, is that we should try to follow the traditions of the British house and the traditions of the British empire in its relations to peoples in every part of the world.
Every time I look at the union jack I am reminded of the fact that the three crosses upon the flag signify one of the most important unions that has ever taken place among the peoples of the world, important not so much because of the numbers who were brought into the union through bringing together the people of England and Scotland and Ireland, but important because of the great influence which it has had upon nations throughout the world. That flag, Mr. Speaker, stands for a union of peoples whether or not their languages, customs and laws are the same.
I might be pardoned standing in this House of Commons of the Dominion of Canada for
[Mr. Gardiner.!
calling attention to this further fact, that we have a great country to the south of us. They, too, have a flag and that flag has thirteen stripes upon it. Each one of those stripes stands for one of the original British colonies on the north American continent that were the foundations upon which that nation has been built. But when you look into the field of blue in the corner of the flag you see forty-eight stars, where at first there were only thirteen. Every time a new state was formed a star was added to the corner until to-day those stars represent forty-eight states, all under one flag, with one literature, if you like, with one set of ideals, with one set of laws, with one common purpose inspiring their people. I could go on and indicate to you, sir, that there is a union of sentiments, a union of ideals, a union of peoples.
Someone said this afternoon that there are more Germans or people of German descent in the United States than anywhere else in the world except perhaps in Germany itself. Someone else might have said that the same is true of Italians; someone else might have said that the same is true of many other nationalities which have gathered under that flag. The very fact that it is true; that many peoples have gathered and been able to live together under one flag, with common customs, with one set of ideals, with one literature, and with a community of sentiment, makes it all the more important that, we in building this great country on the northern half of this continent should unite our people with common ideals by exercising towards all people who were here before the British came that practice of British fair play which the British themselves have extended everywhere throughout the world.

Speaking to this subamendment, I wanted merely to say that I have been amazed, amused and, I am afraid a little pained to see this house spending a day and a half discussing what to many people in Canada is a very trivial aspect of this bill. There are hundreds of people across the prairies to-day who would be very glad to get money, no matter in what language it was printed. Personally, I do not care in what language our bills are printed. Being a Scotsman, I am glad to get a dollar whether it is printed in Siamese or Chinese, provided I can buy something with it.
I want to say to the government that there are people in this country, particularly in western Canada, who possess prejudices and antipathies which are very easy to arouse. We feel that this is a good time to let well enough alone, to let sleeping dogs lie. We have heard a great many recriminations to-night about the 1929 and 1930 elections. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) hurled across the floor in some derision the name of the Regina Daily Star. I wonder if I could remind hon. gentlemen opposite of the fact that in 1929 the editor of the Regina Daily Star, Mr. J. S. Cowper, who wrote such bitter editorials against the use of the French language, was a former Liberal member of the British Columbia legislature. Last August this same gentleman ran as a Liberal candidate in Alberta, and I understand he is now editor of the Edmonton Bulletin. I do not cite these facts for any political reasons because I am not implicated; I cite them to show that this arousing of antipathies in western Canada on the basis of race and religion has not been confined to any one party.

speechtext: What party was that paper supporting when those articles were written? Can you answer that question?

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows without my saying that I had nothing to do with the party which was supported by that paper at that time. I point out that the man who edited the articles was a Liberal prior to that time and is a Liberal again to-day. I point out that antipathies can, be aroused again. It is because we would like to see elections in western Canada fought on economic issues rather than on racial prejudices that I am making this plea at this time. Hon. members from western Canada who sit opposite know as well as I do that it would not be very difficult to arouse in western Canada the same issues that were aroused in 1929 and 1930. It is because we do not want to see them aroused that we are asking the government to reconsider very carefully the step they are taking.
Of what use is it for the Minister of Justice to speak very eloquently about unity when the government places before this house something that will cause disunity in certain parts of Canada? Of what use is it for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to speak about good will and at the same time insert in this bill a clause that will cause ill will in certain comers of Canada? I believe in a homogeneous people. I want to see, as I believe every hon. member wants to see, amity and good will among the Canadian people. But we suggest that good will and homogeneity among the people of Canada can best be brought about at the present time by leaving well enough alone, by letting sleeping dogs lie.
Personally, I would favour carrying on as we are now doing, but as the government has refused to accept the amendment of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber), the hon. member for Vancouver North and I are suggesting that the bills be printed to contain just the word "Canada" and the numeral, along with the signatures of the heads of the Bank of Canada. We believe that this would prevent much of the prejudice and antipathy that are bound to be aroused.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the house for one or two minutes in order to show why we cannot accept the subamendment which has been moved. May I say, first, that I am surprised at the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). The group of which he is a member has always charged the other political parties with a lack of courage, but surely the proposal made is one that would seem to avoid or to evade the straight issue. They want Canada to adopt bank bills which would be entirely emasculated. I do not think a virile country like Canada should adopt such a bank bill.
